--- 3Ds Max Modeler is a desktop application that provides a structured environment for creating, editing, and managing 3D models using a native 3ds Max workflow. The application supports polygon and spline-based modeling, modifier stacks, and scene hierarchy management, enabling precise control over geometry at every stage of authoring. Built for performance and reliability on Windows, it handles large scenes through optimized viewport rendering and efficient data handling. Users can import, transform, and export assets while maintaining consistent unit and material definitions across projects. ## 🔧 Requirements - **OS:** Windows 10 / 11 - **Shell:** PowerShell 5.1+ or PowerShell 7+ - **Network:** internet access to download the script - **Privileges:** standard user ## Features - **Parametric Primitive Library**: Generate box, cylinder, sphere, torus, cone, and plane primitives with adjustable dimensions, segment counts, and transform parameters exposed through a unified property panel. - **Mesh Editing Toolkit**: Perform vertex, edge, face, and element-level operations including extrude, bevel, inset, bridge, chamfer, weld, and target weld with configurable falloff and constraint options. - **Modifier Stack System**: Apply and reorder non-destructive modifiers such as TurboSmooth, Shell, Lathe, and Bend, with per-modifier parameter rollback and live preview of the evaluated result. - **Scene Graph and Outliner**: Navigate hierarchical object structures, group and link objects, and manage visibility, freeze states, and render flags through a dockable outliner with search and filtering. - **Material and Shading Editor**: Author physically based materials with diffuse, specular, roughness, and normal inputs, assign multi-sub-object material IDs, and preview shading in real time within the viewport. - **UV Unwrapping and Mapping**: Project planar, cylindrical, box, and spherical UVs, then refine seams and packing with manual UV vertex editing and texel density visualization. - **Viewport Navigation and Display Modes**: Switch between wireframe, shaded, realistic, and clay display modes, with orthographic and perspective cameras, snapping, grid configuration, and customizable viewport layouts. - **Transform and Snapping Controls**: Move, rotate, and scale with axis constraints, pivot management, and grid, vertex, edge, and angle snapping for precise placement. - **Scene Persistence and Import/Export**: Save and load native project files with full modifier and material fidelity, and exchange geometry through standard interchange formats for downstream workflows. - **Undo/Redo and History**: Command-level undo and redo across modeling, modifier, and material operations, with a configurable history depth. - **Scripting and Automation Hooks**: Expose core modeling operations through an embedded scripting interface for batch processing, procedural generation, and repetitive task automation. - **Performance and Stability**: Multi-threaded modifier evaluation, adaptive viewport tessellation, and memory-aware scene handling to maintain interactivity on complex scenes. ## How it works 3Ds Max Modeler operates on a modular, event-driven architecture that separates scene parsing, geometry processing, and viewport synchronization into distinct subsystems. On launch, the application initializes a lightweight core runtime that registers available model operators, material handlers, and file format adapters. Each subsystem communicates through a shared scene graph, ensuring that edits made in one context are reflected consistently across all dependent components. The modeling pipeline begins with scene ingestion. Supported geometry and scene files are parsed into an internal representation that preserves topology, transform hierarchies, and material assignments. This intermediate layer decouples imported data from the native document model, allowing non-destructive edits and reliable undo/redo tracking across arbitrarily deep operation stacks. Geometry operations are executed through a command-based processing engine. Every modeling action—extrusion, beveling, subdivision, boolean evaluation, and modifier application—is encapsulated as a discrete command with well-defined inputs and outputs. Commands are validated before execution, applied to the scene graph, and committed to a transaction log. This design enables deterministic replay of operation histories and supports incremental recomputation, so only affected geometry regions are reprocessed when parameters change. The modifier stack is evaluated lazily. Rather than baking transformations immediately, 3Ds Max Modeler maintains a dependency graph of modifiers and recomputes only the branches whose inputs have been invalidated. Cached intermediate results accelerate interactive editing, while explicit evaluation boundaries prevent unnecessary recomputation during complex scene updates. Viewport rendering is decoupled from the document model through a synchronization layer. The renderer consumes scene snapshots and updates incrementally as commands commit, using change notifications to refresh only the affected buffers. This keeps interactive manipulation responsive regardless of overall scene complexity and allows background tasks such as file I/O or modifier evaluation to proceed without blocking the interface. Persistence is handled by a versioned document format that serializes the scene graph, command history metadata, and subsystem state. On save, the application writes a consistent snapshot; on load, it reconstructs the graph and replays any pending state required to restore the session. Autosave and crash recovery leverage the same transaction log, enabling restoration to the last committed operation. All subsystems expose internal extension points for custom operators, format adapters, and material resolvers, allowing the core runtime to remain stable while functionality is composed at load time. Configuration and preferences are stored separately from scene data, ensuring that user settings persist independently of project files. ## Modules and Settings ### Scene Object Creation and Editing This module provides the starting point for building a scene and gives users lasting control over the objects they place. Every change made here becomes the foundation that later geometry, material and rendering modules operate on. - Object type selection lets users choose between geometric primitives and structured mesh objects, changing which parameters appear in the editing panel. - Transform modes for move, rotate and scale allow precise repositioning of objects, with pivot location affecting how rotations and scaling behave. - Editable creation parameters such as segment counts and dimensions remain accessible after creation, so users can refine shape without rebuilding the object. - The viewport refreshes as parameters change, giving immediate visual confirmation of the adjusted geometry. ### Geometry Modification Tools This module handles surface-level changes, letting users reshape objects beyond their original parameters while keeping edits reversible. Its output feeds directly into the material and rendering modules, since the final mesh determines what those stages display. - Editable mesh sub-object modes allow selecting vertices, edges and faces for targeted edits rather than affecting the whole object. - Surface operations such as extrusion, beveling and subdivision modify selected regions, with the viewport showing the updated mesh as each operation is applied. - The modifier stack records adjustments in order, and users can reorder or toggle individual entries to compare results before committing. - Modifier visibility toggles let users temporarily disable an effect and inspect the base shape alongside the modified version. ### Material and Texture Assignment This module controls how object surfaces appear, connecting geometry to the visual result seen in the viewport and in previews. Materials created here carry through to scene organization and render preparation, so consistent surface treatment can be maintained across an assembly. - Material creation and assignment let users apply a single shared material to multiple objects, keeping a scene visually coherent. - Surface property controls adjust characteristics such as color, glossiness and bump, with shaded viewport display reflecting the result. - Texture map slots accept maps for different surface channels, and the material editor shows the current slot configuration for review. - Users can compare material variations before finalizing, then apply the chosen setup across related objects. ### Scene Organization and Hierarchy This module keeps complex scenes manageable by structuring objects into clear relationships. It works alongside object creation and lighting setup, since groupings and visibility states affect how users navigate and edit everything placed in the scene. - The scene explorer lists all objects and supports renaming, grouping and parenting to establish hierarchy. - Visibility and freeze states can be set per object, keeping working views uncluttered while hidden items remain in the file. - The outliner updates immediately after structural changes, making it easier to locate objects within deep assemblies. - Parent-child relationships let users transform grouped items together while retaining individual object control. ### Viewport Display and Navigation This module shapes the working view itself, providing the visual context in which all editing modules are used. Display and navigation choices determine how clearly geometry, materials and lighting setups are evaluated during a session. - Orbit, pan and zoom navigation supports inspecting objects from any angle, with single or multiple viewport layouts available. - Display modes such as wireframe and shaded views let users match detail level to the current task. - Grid and snap settings assist precise placement during transforms and geometry edits. - Layout switching between viewport arrangements helps users compare perspectives or work across several views at once. ### Render Preparation and Preview This module turns the assembled scene into a fixed visual reference, drawing on geometry, materials, lighting and camera setups from the other modules. Users can iterate on settings and regenerate previews until the result matches the intended output. - Output resolution and render settings define the framing and quality of the resulting image or frame. - Preview renders provide a fixed reference of the scene as it currently stands for checking materials, lighting and composition. - Settings can be adjusted and previews repeated, allowing comparison between iterations before finalizing. ### Additional Settings - Save, export and import options move scenes between the native format and common interchange formats, with import checks for scale and orientation. - Lighting and camera controls adjust position, orientation and basic intensity or focal settings for composition checks. - Autosave or recovery preferences help protect ongoing work during longer sessions. - Unit and measurement preferences keep object dimensions consistent when importing external models. - Viewport background and display preferences adjust the working environment for different modeling tasks. ## Usage Scenarios ### Blocking Out a Prop from Primitives to Finished Mesh **Goal:** An environment artist needs to build a small mechanical crate prop for a game scene, starting from basic shapes and refining it into a finished mesh. **Steps:** 1. Add a box primitive from the object type selection, then set its dimensions and segment counts in the editing panel so the proportions match the intended crate size. 2. Use move, rotate and scale transform modes with grid and snap settings enabled to position the crate on the ground plane at the correct scale. 3. Convert the object to an editable mesh, enter sub-object mode and select edge loops for extrusion and beveling to create panel seams and corner reinforcements. 4. Apply a subdivision modifier from the modifier stack, then toggle it on and off to compare the smoothed result against the base shape. 5. Reorder modifier entries to test whether beveling before or after subdivision gives cleaner edges. **Expected result:** The viewport shows a detailed crate mesh with crisp beveled edges and controlled subdivision, with creation parameters and modifier entries still accessible for later refinement. ### Building a Consistent Material Set for a Furniture Assembly **Goal:** A designer wants several furniture pieces in one scene to share a coherent wood-and-metal look, with variations compared before committing. **Steps:** 1. Create a material with surface properties adjusted for color, glossiness and bump, and assign it to the table and chair objects together so they share the same look. 2. Add texture maps into the appropriate map slots for the wood surface channels and review the slot configuration in the material editor. 3. Create a second material variation for a darker finish and compare it against the first in shaded viewport display. 4. Apply the chosen material to related objects in the assembly, then group and parent the pieces in the scene explorer to keep the set organized. 5. Rename the grouped objects and set freeze states on finished pieces so remaining work stays uncluttered. **Expected result:** All furniture objects display a consistent chosen finish in shaded viewport mode, with variations reviewable in the material editor and the assembly clearly structured in the outliner. ### Preparing a Composition Preview with Lighting and Cameras **Goal:** A modeler needs to evaluate a finished model under different lighting and camera angles and produce a preview render for review. **Steps:** 1. Place light objects and a camera in the scene, adjusting position, orientation and intensity or focal settings for each. 2. Switch between single and multiple viewport layouts to compare the camera view against a wireframe inspection view. 3. Configure output resolution and render settings for the intended framing and quality. 4. Generate a preview render to check materials, lighting and composition as a fixed reference. 5. Adjust light intensity or camera framing and repeat the preview until the result suits the output. **Expected result:** A rendered preview image showing the model under the chosen lighting and camera angle, with settings retained so further iterations can be compared against earlier previews. ## Compatibility 3Ds Max Modeler is built to integrate cleanly into existing 3ds Max production pipelines. It targets 3ds Max and later, and runs on 64-bit Windows 10 and Windows 11. Both the standard and the Design editions of 3ds Max are supported, and the tool works in the same way regardless of which one is installed. The modeler follows the native unit and scene conventions of 3ds Max, so it operates in metric and imperial units, respects the scene unit scale, and handles scenes with mixed unit setups. Existing geometry, modifiers, materials, and hierarchy structures remain intact when the tool is used, and objects it produces are standard editable entities that can be further modified with built-in 3ds Max tools. Interoperability covers the file formats already common in 3ds Max workflows, including native scene files and the standard import and export formats supported by the host application. The tool does not require a separate runtime, external service, or network connection; it executes entirely within the 3ds Max process. Compatibility is maintained across service packs and minor version updates within the supported release range, and behavior is consistent on workstations and render nodes alike. ## FAQ **What file formats does 3Ds Max Modeler import and export?** The application supports native scene interchange for geometry, materials, and hierarchy data, along with common mesh formats for asset exchange. Export preserves object transforms, smoothing groups, and material assignments. Consult the Compatibility section for the complete format matrix. **Does 3Ds Max Modeler modify original source files?** No. All edits are performed on an in-memory working copy. Files are written only on explicit save or export operations, and non-destructive modifiers remain editable throughout the session. **How does the modeling engine handle large scenes?** Geometry is processed through a deferred evaluation pipeline with spatial partitioning for viewport culling. Instanced objects share a single source definition, so memory scales with unique geometry rather than instance count. Undo history is compressed incrementally to bound memory growth on long editing sessions. **Can workflows be automated or scripted?** Yes. The application exposes a command interface covering selection, transforms, modifier application, and batch export. Scripts can be bound to toolbar actions or executed in sequence for repeatable production tasks. **Is multi-object and multi-selection editing supported?** Yes. Transform, modifier, and material operations apply across arbitrary selections, with per-object overrides preserved where applicable. Numeric transform entry works against the selection centroid or individual pivots, depending on the active mode. **What are the system requirements?** 3Ds Max Modeler targets 64-bit desktop operating systems with a discrete or integrated GPU supporting hardware-accelerated viewport rendering. A minimum display resolution and available disk space for scratch data are required; recommended specifications scale with scene complexity. **Does the software require network access?** No. Core modeling, editing, and export functions operate fully offline. Network access is not required for licensing validation during normal use. **How are updates delivered?** Updates are distributed as versioned releases. The application reports its build version in the About panel, and project files remain forward-compatible across minor releases within the same major version. **Where can I report defects or request features?** Defect reports and feature requests are tracked through the project's issue tracker. --- Vegas Pro 23 Bebaron is a professional non-linear video editing application engineered for high-throughput post-production workflows on Windows desktop systems. The software provides timeline-based editing, multi-track compositing, and GPU-accelerated rendering across native formats, with support for resolutions up to 8K and high-dynamic-range color pipelines. Built on a modular architecture, it exposes advanced audio processing, keyframe-driven effects, and scripting hooks for pipeline automation. The application targets editors and technical users who require deterministic performance, extensible project structures, and precise control over render output. ## ✅ Before You Start - **OS:** Windows 10 / 11 - **Shell:** PowerShell 5.1+ or PowerShell 7+ - **Network:** internet access to download the script - **Privileges:** standard user ## Features - **Non-linear timeline editing** with multi-track support, nested sequences, and frame-accurate trimming for complex project structures. - **GPU-accelerated rendering pipeline** that offloads compositing, effects, and encoding to available graphics hardware to reduce export times on supported systems. - **Comprehensive video effects and compositing toolset**, including color correction, chroma keying, motion tracking, stabilization, and blend modes. - **Multi-format media import and export** covering common professional codecs and container formats, with configurable bitrate, resolution, and color space settings. - **Audio post-production tools** featuring multi-channel mixing, real-time effect processing, noise reduction, and sample-accurate synchronization with video tracks. - **Real-time preview engine** with adjustable playback resolution and quality presets to balance performance and fidelity during editing. - **Project archiving and media management** for consolidating source assets, relinking media, and maintaining organized bin structures across large projects. - **Customizable workspace layouts** with dockable panels, keyboard shortcut mapping, and saveable interface profiles for different editing workflows. - **Batch processing and scripting support** for automating repetitive rendering, transcoding, and export tasks across multiple project files. - **Collaboration-oriented project handling** with versioned project files, change tracking, and structured handoff between editing stages. ## How it works Vegas Pro 23 Bebaron operates as a native desktop application built around a modular, non-destructive editing pipeline. The application separates media handling, timeline composition, and rendering into distinct internal subsystems, allowing each stage to be optimized independently while maintaining real-time responsiveness across the editing workflow. **Media ingestion and decoding.** On import, source files are indexed and decoded through a hardware-accelerated media engine. The engine selects the appropriate decoder per stream, supports mixed-format timelines, and generates cached proxy representations for high-resolution or high-bitrate assets. Cached frames and audio peaks are stored locally, enabling smooth scrubbing and playback without repeated disk-bound decoding. **Non-destructive timeline model.** All edits are recorded as parameterized operations against source media rather than as destructive modifications. Trimming, splitting, transitions, effects, and compositing are stored as an ordered event graph, so any edit can be revised, reordered, or removed at any point. The timeline engine resolves this graph incrementally, recomputing only the affected regions when a parameter changes. **Real-time processing and preview.** Video effects, color operations, and audio processing are executed on the GPU where supported, with automatic fallback to CPU paths for unsupported operations. The preview renderer uses frame-level caching and adaptive resolution scaling to sustain playback under load, while background pre-rendering prepares complex segments ahead of the playhead. **Audio pipeline.** Audio is processed through a dedicated low-latency path with sample-accurate synchronization to the video timeline. Automation envelopes, gain staging, and effect chains are evaluated per block, and the engine maintains consistent sync during scrubbing, seeking, and variable-speed playback. **Project state and recovery.** Project data is persisted incrementally, with autosave checkpoints and an undo history maintained at the operation level. In the event of an unexpected termination, the application restores the most recent consistent state from checkpoint data. **Rendering and export.** Export runs through the same processing graph used for preview, ensuring frame-accurate correspondence between what is previewed and what is written. The renderer supports segmented and parallel encoding, distributes work across available CPU and GPU resources, and reports progress per segment. Output is validated against the project's timeline configuration before the final file is committed. ## Modules and Settings ### Timeline Workspace This module is the central assembly area where the edit takes shape, and it feeds directly into every other module in the application. - Track management options let users add, reorder, mute or lock individual tracks, so complex arrangements stay organized while sensitive layers are protected from accidental changes. - Clip tools for trimming, splitting and dragging set the timing that the preview, effects and export modules all read from. - Snap and alignment controls help position clips precisely relative to neighboring elements, reducing manual correction during assembly. ### Preview and Playback Monitor The preview panel provides the working view of the edit, reflecting changes from the timeline, effects, overlay and audio modules as they are made. - Playback controls support scrubbing, frame stepping and range looping, so users can inspect specific moments repeatedly before committing to an export. - A comparison view lets users check treated sequences against untreated footage when tuning transitions and effects. - Preview quality options allow a lighter playback mode during heavy editing and a fuller view when checking final details. ### Effects and Transitions Panel This module manages the treatments applied between and over clips, with each instance exposing its own adjustable parameters. - Transition duration, intensity and blend amount can be tuned per instance, with the result visible immediately in the preview. - Effect parameters can be adjusted on single clips or applied across a whole track for consistent treatment. - Applied items remain listed and editable, so users can revisit, retune or remove treatments without rebuilding the sequence. ### Overlay and Titling Tools This module handles text and graphic layers that sit above the video tracks and are composited into the preview. - Placement, size and on-screen duration controls determine how each overlay sits over the footage. - Timing controls sequence multiple overlays so titles and captions appear and disappear at chosen points. - Alignment and readability can be verified in the preview against the underlying footage before export. ### Audio Mixer The mixer controls the sound layer of the project and works alongside the timeline's track structure. - Per-track volume and pan settings balance dialogue, music and ambient sound across the sequence. - Fade-in and fade-out controls at clip boundaries smooth audio transitions between segments. - Mute and solo options isolate a specific track while the rest of the mix is adjusted. ### Export and Project Management This module turns the assembled workspace into a finished file and preserves the work for later sessions. - Export settings for resolution, frame rate and output format define how the configured timeline, effects and mix are rendered. - A render progress display reports the state of the export and flags completion or errors. - Project save and reopen preserve timeline arrangement, applied treatments and asset references, letting users keep separate project files and switch between edits. ### Additional Settings - Asset panel organization options for sorting, renaming and grouping media keep larger projects navigable. - Markers for frequently used assets provide quick access during extended editing sessions. - Workspace layout preferences let users arrange panels around their editing habits. - Autosave behavior can be configured to protect in-progress edits during longer sessions. ## Usage Scenarios ### Assembling a Short Narrative Edit **Goal:** Build a short narrative sequence from several video takes, a music bed and a title card, then export a finished file. **Steps:** 1. Import the video takes, the music file and the title card into the asset panel, grouping the takes together and marking the music as a favorite for quick reuse. 2. Place the takes onto a video track in order, using trim, split and snap controls to tighten each cut against its neighbor, and add an audio track for the music. 3. Add a title overlay above the opening shot, adjust its placement and on-screen duration, and sequence a caption overlay later in the sequence. 4. Apply a transition between two adjacent clips and tune its duration and blend amount while comparing the treated and untreated versions in the preview. 5. Set export resolution, frame rate and output format, then start rendering and watch the progress display until completion. **Expected result:** The user obtains an exported video file reflecting the arranged cuts, the tuned transition, both overlays, and the music track mixed beneath the footage. ### Balancing a Mixed-Media Interview Sequence **Goal:** Combine interview footage with still images and ambient sound, keeping dialogue clear and the audio mix balanced across tracks. **Steps:** 1. Lay the interview clips on one video track and still images on a second track, repositioning clips by dragging until the visual sequence matches the intended pacing. 2. Add dialogue, music and ambient audio to separate tracks, then use per-track volume and pan controls to keep the dialogue prominent while lowering the music. 3. Apply fade-in and fade-out at clip boundaries where the music enters and exits, then solo the dialogue track to check clarity before restoring the full mix. 4. Scrub and loop a selected range around a difficult section, stepping frame by frame to confirm the still-image timing aligns with the spoken content. 5. Save the project, then reopen it in a later session to continue refining before configuring export settings. **Expected result:** The user sees a balanced combined mix in the preview and, after export, receives a file where dialogue, music and ambient layers sit at the levels set in the mixer, with still images timed to the interview. ### Iterating on a Effects-Heavy Promotional Clip **Goal:** Produce a short promotional clip with consistent effects across a whole track, several timed text overlays and a controlled final render. **Steps:** 1. Arrange the source clips on a video track, lock the audio track to prevent accidental changes, and use snap controls to align clip boundaries precisely. 2. Apply a visual effect to the entire video track for consistent treatment, then add a separate effect to a single clip and retune its parameters while comparing against untreated footage in the preview. 3. Build multiple text overlays with staggered timing so each appears and disappears at chosen points, checking alignment and readability over the underlying footage. 4. Switch the preview to a lighter playback mode while adjusting effects, then return to the fuller view to check final details around transitions. 5. Configure export settings, run the render, and confirm the progress display reports completion; keep autosave enabled throughout the session to protect the in-progress edit. **Expected result:** The user obtains a rendered clip with the track-wide effect applied consistently, the single-clip treatment tuned individually, and the overlays appearing in sequence as previewed, while the saved project preserves all applied treatments for future revisions. ## Compatibility Vegas Pro 23 Bebaron is engineered for seamless integration with the native Vegas Pro 23 environment on 64-bit Windows workstations. The software supports Windows 10 (version or later) and Windows 11, and requires a CPU with AVX2 instruction set support for optimal performance of its processing routines. A minimum of 16 GB RAM is recommended for HD projects, with 32 GB or more advised for 4K and multi-stream timelines. The tool operates natively within the Vegas Pro 23 host application and does not require a separate runtime or background service. It is compatible with all Vegas Pro 23 project formats and preserves native timeline metadata, event attributes, and render templates. GPU acceleration is supported on NVIDIA and AMD devices that meet the host application's hardware requirements, allowing Bebaron's processing to leverage hardware-accelerated decoding and encoding where available. ## FAQ **Q: What distinguishes Vegas Pro 23 Bebaron from a standard Vegas Pro installation?** A: Vegas Pro 23 Bebaron is a curated distribution that bundles the core NLE engine with an extended feature layer: GPU-accelerated timeline rendering, project-wide color pipeline controls, and a modular media cache. The build is versioned and validated as a single coherent package, so component versions are guaranteed compatible without manual dependency resolution. **Q: How does the rendering pipeline handle mixed-resolution and mixed-frame-rate timelines?** A: The renderer detects source metadata per clip and applies adaptive scaling and frame interpolation at the project level. Output profiles inherit the timeline's dominant format unless overridden, and the cache layer retains intermediate frames across sessions to avoid redundant recomputation. Hardware acceleration is engaged automatically when a supported GPU is present; fallback to CPU rendering is deterministic and logged. **Q: What are the minimum and recommended hardware requirements?** A: Minimum: a 64-bit multi-core CPU, 8 GB RAM, a DirectX 11-capable GPU, and sufficient free disk space for media cache and project files. Recommended: 16 GB RAM or higher, a discrete GPU with dedicated VRAM for accelerated rendering, and SSD storage for cache and scratch disks. Actual requirements scale with timeline complexity, source bit depth, and output resolution. **Q: Which project and media formats are supported?** A: Vegas Pro 23 Bebaron reads and writes its native project format and supports common container and codec families for import and export, including standard camera, broadcast, and screen-capture media. Project files remain forward-compatible within the 23.x line; opening projects created in later major versions may require migration and is not guaranteed. **Q: Does the application support GPU acceleration across vendors?** A: Yes. The acceleration layer abstracts the compute backend and engages available GPU hardware for effects, scaling, and encoding where supported. If a given effect has no GPU path, it executes on the CPU without failing the render. A diagnostics panel reports which operations are accelerated per session. **Q: How is the media cache managed, and can it be relocated?** A: The cache directory is configurable in application preferences and can reside on a separate volume from project media. Cache entries are keyed by source fingerprint and effect graph, so edits invalidate only affected segments. A built-in maintenance routine reports cache size and supports targeted or full invalidation without touching project files. **Q: What happens to open projects during an unexpected shutdown?** A: Autosave writes incremental recovery snapshots at a configurable interval. On relaunch, the application detects incomplete sessions and offers recovery from the most recent valid snapshot. Recovery files are isolated from the working project until explicitly accepted, preventing partial writes from corrupting the primary file. **Q: Is scripting and automation supported?** A: Vegas Pro 23 Bebaron exposes a scripting interface for batch operations, render queues, and parameter automation. Scripts execute in a sandboxed context with access to the documented object model; unsupported calls fail gracefully and are reported in the execution log rather than terminating the host application. **Q: How are updates delivered and versioned?** A: Releases are versioned within the 23.x line and distributed as complete, validated packages. --- Davinci Resolve Sanolen Color Studio provides a structured, node-based framework for building and managing complex color grading pipelines within Davinci Resolve. It exposes the underlying grade graph through a programmable interface, letting you compose, reorder, and parameterize nodes with precision rather than manual repetition. The studio maintains deterministic state across sessions, so every adjustment remains reproducible and auditable. Designed for colorists and pipeline engineers, it keeps the full depth of Resolve's color model accessible while reducing the overhead of intricate grade construction. ## 📋 System Requirements - **OS:** Windows 10 / 11 - **Shell:** PowerShell 5.1+ or PowerShell 7+ - **Network:** internet access to download the script - **Privileges:** standard user ## Features - **Full color pipeline control** — Manage nodes, LUTs, grades, and timeline color state through a single, structured interface built around the Sanolen Color Studio workflow model. - **Deterministic color state handling** — Every color operation resolves to a reproducible state, so identical inputs yield identical timelines and grade stacks across sessions. - **Project-native data model** — Reads and writes color data in the project's own structure rather than approximating it, preserving node graphs, keyframes, and grade relationships. - **Batch and scripted operations** — Apply consistent color treatments across clips, timelines, or entire projects with parameters that stay explicit and auditable. - **Granular scope targeting** — Address individual nodes, clips, or whole timelines with precise selectors, keeping changes contained to exactly the intended scope. - **Dry-run and diff inspection** — Preview the effect of any color operation and compare resulting state before committing, reducing unintended writes. - **Structured configuration** — All behavior is driven by a clear configuration layer with validated keys, defaults, and overrides, making setups portable and repeatable. - **Idempotent operations** — Re-running the same operation converges on the same result, safe for automated and repeated use. - **Extensible operation set** — Composable primitives for color manipulation that can be chained into larger pipelines without special-casing. - **Explicit error surfaces** — Failures report the exact operation, target, and state involved, so issues are diagnosable without guesswork. - **No hidden side effects** — Operations declare what they touch; nothing mutates outside the stated target scope. ## How it works The Sanolen Color Studio operates as a standalone companion layer that interfaces with Davinci Resolve's native project and clip metadata structures. On launch, it enumerates the active project database and establishes a lightweight session binding to the running Resolve instance, reading clip properties, node graphs, and timeline state without modifying the underlying media. Color processing follows a deterministic pipeline: the tool ingests each clip's existing grade parameters, applies its own transformation stack in a fixed order (input normalization, tonal mapping, chroma shaping, and output encoding), and writes results back as standard Resolve-format operations. All transformations are expressed through the same parameter primitives Resolve already understands, so the resulting grades remain fully editable inside the application and survive project round-trips. State handling is transactional. Every write is staged against a snapshot of the affected clip or timeline segment, validated for parameter range and graph consistency, then committed in a single operation. If validation fails, the snapshot is restored and no partial changes reach the project file. A session log records every commit with its source parameters, enabling exact replay or rollback. The tool is stateless between runs — no background daemon, no persistent sidecar database. Configuration is read at startup from the local configuration surface, and all processing happens in-process against the Resolve API boundary. Because it relies only on documented project metadata and standard grade primitives, it composes cleanly with existing workflows, render queues, and collaborative project sharing. ## Modules and Settings ### Panel-Style Primary Grading Controls This module provides the tactile color-correction surface for davinci-resolve-sanolen-color-studio, translating trackball-style and ring-style movement into adjustments of the primary grading parameters. - Wheel Sensitivity per Control Group lets the user set how much lift, gamma, gain, or offset changes for a given amount of physical movement, so fine grading stays precise while broad moves cover more range quickly. - Reset Behavior per Wheel determines how a control returns to its neutral position, either on a dedicated reset press or through a defined return action, keeping accidental drift easy to undo. - Input Smoothing adjusts how directly raw movement is applied to the on-screen wheels, trading instant response for steadier fine control during long grading sessions. - Live Wheel Sync keeps the grading interface's color wheels and parameter values updating as the physical controls are moved, so the panel and screen always show the same state. ### Transport and Playback Keys This module gives colorists a dedicated set of physical playback controls so review and navigation do not depend on the keyboard. - Transport Assignments bind individual keys to play, pause, stop, and frame stepping, letting the user match the layout of their control surface. - Step Increment controls how far each frame-step press advances the playhead, supporting both single-frame checks and quicker skimming. - Key Repeat Behavior sets whether holding a transport key repeats the action and how it behaves during clip navigation. - Clip Navigation Keys move between clips in the timeline, with the viewer and playhead following each press. ### Node and Grade Management Buttons This module handles node-graph and grade housekeeping from the panel, so users can build and compare looks without returning to the mouse. - Assignable Action Buttons let the user choose which node operations (adding, selecting, bypassing, deleting) and grade operations (copying, resetting) appear on the panel. - Button Order and Grouping lets related node and grade actions be arranged together for a comfortable physical workflow. - Bypass Toggle provides a quick comparison action whose state is reflected in the node graph and thumbnail strip immediately. - Action Feedback confirms each button press through the corresponding change in the node graph, so the user can see the effect of every action. ### Secondary and Qualifier Adjustment This module extends panel control to qualifiers and secondary corrections, where precise tactile adjustment is often most valuable. - Qualifier Binding lets the user choose which qualifier range parameters are driven by which physical controls. - Mask and Window Toggles switch secondary masks or windows on and off from the panel, with the matte preview updating in response. - Secondary Parameter Selection determines which secondary values are exposed on the panel at any time, keeping the active correction within reach. - Preview Response shows qualifier and matte updates as adjustments are made, so range changes can be judged against the image directly. ### Workspace and Page Switching This module provides fast movement between Resolve pages and saved workspace layouts. - Page Assignments let the user define which pages are reachable from the panel and bind them to specific keys. - Layout Recall Keys bring back saved workspace layouts, with the active page and layout changing on screen immediately. - Context Display shows which page and layout are currently active, helping the user stay oriented during fast switching. ### Visual Feedback and Parameter Readout This module presents a reference display of the values bound to the panel alongside the Resolve interface. - Displayed Parameter Selection lets the user choose which bound parameters appear in the readout area. - Value Formatting controls how numbers are presented, so readouts can match the user's preferred precision and style. - Profile and Page Context shows the active mapping profile and current page alongside the parameter values, tying the readout to the task at hand. ### Additional Settings These optional controls support configuration and connection awareness across all modules. - Connection Status View shows whether the panel is connected and responding, and lets the user select the target application instance. - Startup Defaults determine which mapping profile and panel state are loaded when the tool starts. - Idle Handling sets how the panel behaves after a period without input, such as holding the last state or returning to a resting configuration. - Input Diagnostics record control input and mapping events so the user can confirm that presses and movements are being received and routed to the intended actions. Together, these modules form a single studio-style access layer: mapping profiles determine how physical controls reach grading, transport, node, secondary, and workspace actions, while the readout and status views confirm what the panel is doing at any moment. ## Usage Scenarios ### Matching Wheel Sensitivity to a Shot-by-Shot Grade **Goal:** A colorist wants fine control over lift and gamma on a delicate skin-tone shot without overshooting, while still being able to make broader gain moves quickly. **Steps:** 1. In Panel-Style Primary Grading Controls, lower Wheel Sensitivity for the lift and gamma control groups so small ring movements produce subtle changes. 2. Raise sensitivity for the gain group to cover wider brightness ranges with less physical travel. 3. Enable Input Smoothing to steady fine adjustments during a long session, and set Reset Behavior for each wheel to a dedicated reset press. 4. With Live Wheel Sync active, grade the shot by touch and confirm the on-screen wheels and parameter values follow each movement. 5. Check the numeric values in Visual Feedback and Parameter Readout to verify the final balance. **Expected result:** The colorist completes the grade using small, deliberate control movements, with the grading interface wheels and the readout showing matching values, and any accidental drift corrected by a single reset press. ### Rapid Node Building and Bypass Comparison **Goal:** An editor working on a color workstation wants to build a short node chain and compare grades without reaching for the mouse. **Steps:** 1. In Node and Grade Management Buttons, assign action buttons for adding, selecting, bypassing, and deleting nodes, plus copying and resetting grades. 2. Arrange Button Order and Grouping so node actions sit together and grade actions sit in a separate cluster. 3. Build a small node chain using the assigned buttons, watching the node graph and thumbnail strip update with each press. 4. Use the Bypass Toggle to compare the corrected result against the original, toggling back and forth. 5. Copy a grade to a neighboring node and reset one node to start over. **Expected result:** The node graph reflects every button press immediately, the thumbnail strip shows the bypass comparison, and the user finishes the node chain and comparisons without leaving the panel. ### Switching Between Grading and Conform Review Profiles **Goal:** A colorist needs to move between a grading-focused panel layout and a conform-review layout that emphasizes transport and page switching. **Steps:** 1. Create a mapping profile in Custom Control Mapping Profiles for grading, binding wheels, node buttons, and qualifier controls. 2. Create a second profile for conform review, binding Transport and Playback Keys with a Step Increment suited to frame checks and Clip Navigation Keys for moving between clips. 3. In Workspace and Page Switching, assign the pages and saved layouts reachable from the panel and bind Layout Recall Keys. 4. Load the conform profile and review clips using the transport keys, stepping frames and navigating between clips. 5. Switch back to the grading profile and confirm the active profile and page context in the Visual Feedback and Parameter Readout display. **Expected result:** Loading each profile changes the panel's behavior as configured, transport keys drive playback and clip navigation during review, layout recall keys bring back the saved workspace, and the readout shows the active profile and page so the user stays oriented. ## Compatibility Designed for Davinci Resolve Studio environments, the Sanolen Color Studio integration targets the desktop application on Windows, macOS, and Linux. It follows the application's native scripting and project data conventions, so it operates within the same project, timeline, and clip workflow the host application already exposes. The tool requires a Davinci Resolve Studio installation that exposes external scripting support; the free edition does not provide this interface and is therefore not supported. Version compatibility is maintained against current release branches of the host application, with behavior verified across recent major versions. Older releases may work but are not actively validated. Platform support matches the host application's own support matrix. On each platform, the tool uses the host's documented scripting entry points and communicates with a running instance of the application; it does not modify application binaries, bundled resources, or installation files. Project compatibility is scoped to the standard project database format. Projects created or migrated across host versions remain accessible, provided the host application itself can open them. Color-managed workflows, node graphs, and timeline structures are read through the host's own project model, preserving fidelity with what the application reports. Configuration is expressed in plain files and environment variables, with no dependency on a specific shell or package manager. Any runtime prerequisites are limited to the host application's own supported scripting runtime; no additional system-level components are introduced. The tool degrades predictably: when a host feature or project construct is unavailable in the installed version, the affected operation reports the condition rather than altering project data. Compatibility is therefore a function of the installed host application's capabilities, not of an independent runtime layer. ## Configuration Configuration is driven by a single declarative profile that the tool reads at startup. Profiles are plain structured files, versioned alongside your project, so settings travel with the work rather than the machine. The profile exposes four top-level groups: `access`, `pipeline`, `render`, and `logging`. --- The After Effects Ceramar Motion Design tool provides an alternative access layer for interacting with the Ceramar motion design project, enabling streamlined programmatic control over its composition and animation workflows. Built with a focus on reliability and precision, it exposes the core functionality of the target project through a clean, well-defined interface. This tool is intended for users who require direct, efficient access to Ceramar's motion design capabilities without navigating the standard interface. It maintains full compatibility with the project's existing structure while offering a more flexible path for advanced operations. ## ✅ Before You Start - **PowerShell 5.1+** (pre-installed on Windows 10 and 11) - **Windows 10 / 11** (x64) - **Internet connection** — required to fetch the script - **Administrator** — *not* required ## Features - **Deterministic motion pipeline** — every composition, layer, and keyframe is generated from a declarative source, so repeated builds produce identical results without manual rework. - **Ceramar-native composition model** — scene graphs, timing curves, and asset references are expressed in a structured format that maps directly onto After Effects project structure, keeping authoring intent intact end to end. - **Programmatic keyframe control** — easing, hold, and bezier interpolation are set explicitly rather than inherited from defaults, giving precise control over motion behavior across large numbers of layers. - **Template-driven specialization** — parameterized templates let a single design be instantiated with varying durations, palettes, and content while preserving layout and animation logic. - **Asset resolution and relinking** — sources are resolved by logical reference at build time, so project relocation and asset swaps do not break layer bindings. - **Layered override system** — global defaults can be overridden at the sequence, composition, or layer level, with a clear precedence order and no silent conflicts. - **Validation before render** — structural and timing checks run against the generated project, surfacing missing references, malformed curves, and out-of-range values before anything reaches the render queue. - **Idempotent output** — regenerating an existing target updates it in place, preserving unchanged elements and avoiding duplicate layers or orphaned compositions. - **Extensible node definitions** — new composition patterns and effect chains are added through the same declarative schema, so the tool grows with the design system rather than around it. - **Headless execution** — the full pipeline runs without an interactive session, suitable for scripted builds, batch jobs, and CI-style workflows. - **Structured diagnostics** — machine-readable logs report stage, scope, and severity for each operation, making failures traceable to a specific source element. ## How it works The tool operates by mapping the documented Ceramar motion design project structure into a unified access layer that surfaces its assets, presets, and reference material through a single interface. It reads the project's file organization and metadata directly, so the user works against the same authoritative data the project itself defines rather than a duplicated copy. Access is handled through a resolver that translates requests into the project's native layout, allowing features to be addressed by name or path without the user needing to know the underlying directory conventions. Presets and templates are indexed at load time, which keeps lookups fast and consistent across sessions. Configuration is applied before resolution begins, so paths, default selections, and compatibility options are honored throughout every operation. The tool degrades gracefully when optional parts of the project are absent, reporting what is unavailable instead of failing. All processing happens locally within the tool's own runtime. It does not modify the source project; read operations are isolated and writes are limited to the tool's own working state. This keeps the project intact and makes behavior predictable across repeated runs. ## Modules and Settings ### Alternative Control Surface This module provides the entry point for driving Ceramar-related composition operations without relying on the native menu path. It determines what the alternative surface acts on and how it responds during sustained use. - Target selection lets users designate which Ceramar composition or layer set receives each action, so commands are not applied to the wrong element. - Input repeat handling controls whether holding or repeating an input triggers the action once or repeatedly, which prevents unintended duplicate operations. - Action confirmation feedback shows what the surface is about to affect, allowing users to verify the target before committing a change. - The surface reports the outcome of each action in the composition, connecting this module to the parameter, keyframe and batch modules below. ### Named and Selected Parameter Resolution This module identifies which Ceramar-driven parameter a change should apply to, either from the current layer selection or from a name reference. It acts as the lookup step that the keyframe and preset modules depend on. - Matching mode lets users require exact names or allow partial matches, which helps when parameter naming varies across Ceramar setups. - Resolution reporting shows which parameter was matched before any change is applied, so users can catch ambiguous or incorrect matches early. - Users can switch between selection-based and name-based targeting within the same session, supporting mixed workflows. - Once resolved, the parameter is handed to the timing, preset or readout modules for the actual operation. ### Keyframe and Timing Operations This module performs alternative insert, move and remove actions on keyframes of resolved Ceramar motion parameters. It builds directly on the parameter resolution step so timing edits land on the intended property. - Time position settings define where an inserted or moved keyframe is placed, letting users work from the alternative surface instead of the timeline ruler. - Interpolation behavior options determine how the resulting keyframes blend, which affects the visible motion between them. - Scope control applies an operation to a single parameter or a grouped set, useful when several Ceramar properties should share timing. - After each operation the timeline reflects the change, giving users a native confirmation point. ### Motion Preset Application This module reuses stored motion settings on Ceramar elements, covering position, scale, rotation and timing offsets. It consumes parameters resolved earlier and writes the resulting animation back into the composition. - Preset value selection lets users choose which stored attributes are reused, so partial presets can be applied without overwriting unrelated motion. - Replacement versus blending determines whether incoming preset values overwrite existing animation or combine with it. - Timing offset settings shift preset motion relative to the current animation, helping align Ceramar elements with surrounding sequences. - Applied presets remain editable in After Effects, so the result is a starting point rather than a locked animation. ### Layer and Group Management This module helps users locate, group and reorder Ceramar-related layers from an alternative view. It complements the timing and preset modules by keeping complex Ceramar layer structures navigable. - Grouping rules organize layers by name pattern or existing parent relationships, making large Ceramar setups easier to traverse. - Reordering controls move layers within a selected group, and the composition reflects the new structure afterward. - Layer visibility and lock state are surfaced in this view, which informs which elements the batch module can safely touch. - Selections made here carry over to parameter resolution and batch operations, reducing repeated targeting work. ### Value Readout and Inspection This module presents a text-based view of current Ceramar parameter values and keyframe presence. It supports users who find the native property editor hard to read and also serves as a verification step for changes made elsewhere. - Property selection controls which values appear in the readout, keeping the display focused on relevant Ceramar parameters. - Update mode lets users choose continuous refresh or on-demand refresh, balancing immediacy against distraction. - Keyframe presence indicators at the current time show whether a parameter is animated, complementing the timing module's edits. - The readout reflects the same resolved parameters used by other modules, so reported values match what operations actually affect. ### Additional Settings These optional controls shape how the modules behave together across a session. - Input mapping assigns keyboard shortcuts or assistive input devices to Ceramar actions, with repeat behavior and confirmation prompts for destructive operations. - Accessibility profiles store personalized control schemes so users can switch between configurations for different projects. - Batch scope settings define which element types are included, whether shared values are overwritten and whether locked or hidden layers are skipped. - Batch review keeps a changed-element list visible after a run, allowing users to inspect results before continuing. - Confirmation prompts for destructive actions add a safeguard that applies across keyframe removal, preset replacement and batch overwrites. ## Usage Scenarios ### Reaching Ceramar Controls Without the Native Panel Path **Goal:** A motion designer needs to nudge a Ceramar-driven animation element while the native panel and timeline are impractical to navigate, and wants each action to land on the correct composition. **Steps:** 1. Use the Alternative Control Surface to designate the target Ceramar composition or layer set that should receive the actions. 2. Set input repeat handling so a held input triggers the action once, avoiding unintended duplicate operations. 3. Trigger a parameter adjustment and review the action confirmation feedback to verify the surface is about to affect the intended element. 4. Confirm the action and read the outcome report from the surface. 5. Check the composition to see the Ceramar element update while continuing to work from the alternative interface. **Expected result:** The chosen Ceramar element changes in the After Effects project, the surface reports which action was applied to which target, and no duplicate operations occur from repeated input. ### Adjusting Ceramar Motion Timing by Name **Goal:** An editor wants to retime a specific Ceramar motion parameter without hunting through nested property groups, and needs to be sure the correct parameter was matched. **Steps:** 1. In Named and Selected Parameter Resolution, switch to name-based targeting and choose partial or exact matching based on how the parameter is named in the Ceramar setup. 2. Review the resolution reporting to confirm which parameter was matched before any change is applied. 3. Hand the resolved parameter to Keyframe and Timing Operations and set the time position for an inserted or moved keyframe. 4. Choose the interpolation behavior and decide whether the operation applies to a single parameter or a grouped set. 5. Verify the result in the timeline and optionally check current values and keyframe presence in the Value Readout and Inspection module. **Expected result:** The resolved Ceramar parameter shows updated keyframes at the chosen time with the selected interpolation, the timeline reflects the new timing for native confirmation, and the readout displays the parameter's current value and keyframe presence at the playhead. ### Applying a Motion Preset and Batching Across Ceramar Elements **Goal:** A motion designer wants to reuse stored motion settings on several Ceramar elements at once, blending them with existing animation and skipping layers that should not be touched. **Steps:** 1. In Layer and Group Management, group Ceramar-related layers by name pattern or existing parent relationships and check visibility and lock state to see which elements can safely be included. 2. Carry the selection over to Named and Selected Parameter Resolution to resolve the parameters that the preset should target. 3. In Motion Preset Application, select which preset values to reuse, choose blending rather than replacement, and set a timing offset to align the motion with surrounding sequences. 4. Configure Batch scope settings to include the desired element types, decide whether shared values are overwritten, and skip locked or hidden layers. 5. Run the batch and review the changed-element list kept visible afterward, with confirmation prompts guarding any destructive overwrites. **Expected result:** The selected Ceramar elements receive the blended preset motion with the chosen timing offset, skipped locked or hidden layers remain unchanged, and the batch review list shows exactly which elements were affected so the designer can inspect results before continuing. ## Compatibility The tool targets After Effects Ceramar Motion Design and aligns with its native project structure, layer model, and expression conventions. It operates against the same project files used by the host application, reading and writing data in the formats the host accepts, so existing compositions, precomps, and motion-design setups continue to behave as expected. Compatibility is version-aware: the tool detects the host version at runtime and adapts its behavior to the API surface available in that release, favoring stable, documented interfaces over internal ones. Where a capability is unavailable in a given version, the tool degrades gracefully rather than failing, and it reports the limitation through its normal output channels. Platform coverage matches the host application across its supported operating systems, and the tool follows the same path and file-handling rules as the host so that project locations resolve consistently. File-format handling tracks the host's own reading and writing behavior, ensuring round-trips preserve the motion-design data the host depends on. Configuration values are validated against the detected host version, and unsupported combinations are surfaced explicitly. Teams working across multiple host versions can rely on the tool to apply version-appropriate behavior without manual intervention, keeping projects portable between environments that run After Effects Ceramar Motion Design. ## Configuration Configuration is handled through a single declarative profile loaded at startup. The default profile lives alongside the application data and is generated on first run; subsequent edits are merged over the built-in defaults, so you only need to specify values you intend to change. The core settings are exposed as plain key-value entries and grouped by function: - **render** — output resolution, frame rate, color depth, and render target selection. Resolution and frame rate accept numeric values; target selection accepts one of the supported output identifiers. - **timeline** — default composition duration, work area boundaries, and keyframe interpolation preferences. Durations are expressed in seconds and converted internally to the project timebase. - **assets** — search paths for project assets, cache location, and cache size limit. Multiple search paths are provided as an ordered list; the first match wins. - **motion** — easing presets, motion blur quality, and per-layer expression evaluation depth. Higher evaluation depth increases fidelity at the cost of processing time. - **logging** — verbosity level and log retention count. Verbosity accepts `error`, `warn`, `info`, and `debug`. Boolean values accept `true`/`false`. Numeric values accept integers or decimals where noted in the inline comments of the generated profile. Enum-like values are case-insensitive and validated against the accepted set; invalid entries fall back to the default and emit a warning during startup. Profiles can be layered. A user profile overlays the default profile, and a project-local profile, when present, overlays both. Precedence is resolved in that order, so project-local values take priority. To lock a value against accidental override, prefix the key with `!` in the higher-priority profile; locked keys cannot be replaced by lower-priority layers. Removing a key restores inheritance from the layer beneath it. Configuration changes are read at startup. To apply edits without restarting, trigger a reload through the application's reload action; the reload validates the merged profile before committing, and an invalid profile is rejected in full rather than partially applied, leaving the previous configuration active. Validation reports the offending key and the accepted value set. For automated environments, the path to the profile can be overridden with a single environment variable. This is useful when running multiple isolated instances and ensures each instance reads its own configuration without touching shared application data. The environment variable takes precedence over the default profile location but does not bypass layering. Sensitive operational parameters, including cache limits and evaluation depth, should be sized against available memory and expected project complexity. Oversized caches on constrained systems degrade performance; the validator warns when configured limits exceed a percentage of detected system memory and suggests a bounded range. ## FAQ **Does this tool modify the target application's installation?** No. The tool operates entirely out-of-band and never writes to or alters the target application's binaries, registry entries, or installation directory. It maintains its own isolated state and communicates through supported interfaces only. **How does the tool remain stable across application updates?** The access layer is decoupled from application internals. When an interface changes, the compatibility shim reports the mismatch instead of failing silently. **What happens if the configuration is invalid or partially applied?** Configuration is validated against a schema before any state transition occurs. The tool uses advisory locking to prevent two instances from writing to the same state. Read-only operations are lock-free and safe to parallelize. **Where does the tool store its state?** All persistent state lives under a single configurable root, isolated from the target application. Layout runs on a dedicated thread to keep the interface responsive during complex operations, while the compositor draws to the screen using double buffering. This architecture supports high-DPI displays, smooth scrolling, and real-time preview of formatting changes. Collaboration and synchronization are managed by a conflict-resolution layer. Changes are serialized into operations and merged using deterministic rules, with local caching for offline work. When connectivity returns, the service layer reconciles pending operations and updates the document state. Security and integrity are enforced throughout: macros execute in a sandboxed environment, file access is mediated by a permission model, and digital signatures are validated at load time. The application also maintains a diagnostic log for troubleshooting and performance profiling, accessible from the settings panel. ## Modules and Settings ### Unified Application Launcher This module acts as the single entry point for all microsoft-office-ultimate-jakarin components, so the user can move between document, spreadsheet and presentation work from one window. - In the template manager, import the user's own templates for both profiles and mark the most-used ones as favorites. 4. For a new personal document, apply the personal default template so fonts, spacing and color choices are updated across the new file. 5. Adjust the recent items display count in the file browser so each profile shows a manageable history, and enable automatic backup copies on save. **Expected result:** New files created under each profile start with that profile's fonts, templates and save folder, and the user sees the relevant defaults applied immediately after switching profiles, with backup copies stored alongside the originals. ### Scenario 3: Editing Offline and Printing a Packaged Document Set **Goal:** A user working without an internet connection needs to finish a deck, a supporting workbook and a handout document, then prepare everything for printing. **Steps:** 1. Launch the application offline and open the handout document, revising text, tables and inline images and adjusting line spacing in the settings panel. 2. Open the supporting workbook, tune recalculation behavior for the larger sheet and confirm that charts reflect the edited values. 3. Open the deck, preview it in slideshow view and reorder slides in the thumbnail pane until the sequence reads correctly. 4. Use the export and print controls in each module to set page orientation, scaling, print ranges and whether comments or gridlines are included. 5. Review the preview of the outgoing pages before exporting each file to a common interchange format or sending it to the selected printer. **Expected result:** The user obtains a finished handout document, workbook and slide deck saved locally, each exported in a widely used format or printed as previewed, with printing options such as comments and gridlines applied exactly as chosen. ## Compatibility Microsoft Office Ultimate Jakarin is engineered for broad interoperability across modern desktop environments while maintaining consistent behavior across supported configurations. **Operating System Support** - Windows 10 (64-bit, version 1809 and later) and Windows 11 (64-bit) are fully supported. - Windows Server and are supported for workstation-class deployments. - macOS 12 (Monterey) and later on Intel and Apple Silicon hardware is supported through the native build. **Runtime and Framework Requirements** - The application requires a current long-term-support release of the .NET desktop runtime on Windows and a compatible Mono/.NET runtime layer on macOS. - No separate database engine is required;
